nodes.desc: Six proof problems over two days, where one solved completely beats three half-written. Everything below this converges here, because a paper at this level never tells you which of the four subjects it is testing.

nodes.name: The Method
nodes.desc: Turning a question into something an experiment could actually settle, with a control and a prediction that could fail. The willingness to be wrong is the part that makes it work.

nodes.name: Asking a Testable Question
nodes.desc: Narrowing an interest into something with a measurable answer. "Does this work" becomes "does this change that, by how much, compared with what" before any apparatus is touched.

nodes.name: Units & Dimensions
nodes.desc: Every quantity carries a unit, and units follow through a calculation like algebra. Checking that they come out right catches more mistakes than rechecking the arithmetic.

nodes.name: Measurement
nodes.desc: Getting a number off an instrument and knowing how much of it to believe. Precision, accuracy and uncertainty are three different things, and reporting all three honestly is the skill.

nodes.name: Uncertainty & Error
nodes.desc: Every measurement is a range rather than a value, and the ranges combine through a calculation in predictable ways. A result quoted without one is not yet a scientific result.

nodes.name: Data & Graphs
nodes.desc: Turning readings into a picture that shows the relationship. Which variable goes on which axis, and whether a line through the points is justified at all, are decisions rather than conventions.

nodes.name: Variables & Controls
nodes.desc: Changing one thing, holding the rest still, and knowing what you failed to hold still. A result from an experiment with two things changing at once cannot be attributed to either.

nodes.name: Laboratory Practice
nodes.desc: Working safely and repeatably: hazards read before starting, equipment used properly, and everything recorded as it happens rather than afterwards from memory.

nodes.name: Recording Results
nodes.desc: A notebook somebody else could repeat the work from, including the readings that went wrong. Tidying data as you record it is how the interesting anomaly gets lost.

nodes.name: Models
nodes.desc: A simplified description that predicts something. Every model is wrong in some respect on purpose, and knowing which simplification you made is what tells you where it will fail.

nodes.name: Scale & Orders of Magnitude
nodes.desc: Estimating roughly before calculating precisely, and noticing when an answer is a thousand times too large. Scientists check a result against a rough estimate before they check the arithmetic.

nodes.name: Statistics for Science
nodes.desc: Deciding whether a difference is bigger than the noise, and how large it is. The effect size answers whether it matters; significance only answers whether it is probably there.

nodes.name: Weighing Evidence
nodes.desc: One study is a data point rather than a finding. Sample size, design and whether anybody has reproduced it decide how much weight a result can carry.

nodes.name: Reproducibility
nodes.desc: Somebody else getting your result from your description. It is the mechanism that makes science self-correcting, and it works only when methods are published in enough detail to follow.

nodes.name: Scientific Writing
nodes.desc: Method, results and discussion kept strictly apart, so a reader can disagree with your interpretation while accepting your data. The separation is the discipline, not the format.

nodes.name: Reading & Reviewing Papers
nodes.desc: Reading the methods before the abstract, and the figures before the conclusion. Peer review filters rather than verifies, which is why a published paper is a claim and not a fact.

nodes.name: Research Ethics
nodes.desc: Consent, welfare, honest reporting and declaring who paid for the work. Presenting an exploratory finding as though it had been the hypothesis all along is the commonest quiet dishonesty in the field.

nodes.name: Communicating Science
nodes.desc: Explaining a result to people who will not read the paper, without overstating it. Most public misunderstanding of science is generated at exactly this step rather than in the laboratory.

nodes.name: Kinematics
nodes.desc: Describing motion without asking what causes it: position, velocity, acceleration and the equations linking them. Getting comfortable that acceleration is a change in velocity rather than a large velocity is half the battle.

nodes.name: Vectors in Physics
nodes.desc: Quantities with a direction, and splitting them into components along axes you chose. Choosing the axes well turns a two-dimensional problem into two one-dimensional ones.

nodes.name: Newton Laws
nodes.desc: Force changes motion, forces come in pairs, and a body with no net force keeps doing exactly what it was doing. The third law is the one people state correctly and apply to the wrong body.

nodes.name: Free-Body Diagrams
nodes.desc: Drawing one object and every force acting on it, and nothing else. It is not a study aid; on most problems it is where the answer comes from, and skipping it is why the algebra goes wrong.

nodes.name: Friction & Circular Motion
nodes.desc: Contact forces that resist sliding, and the fact that going round a corner at constant speed is still accelerating. Centrifugal force does not appear in any of these diagrams, and that is the point.

nodes.name: Work & Energy
nodes.desc: A bookkeeping quantity that is never created or destroyed, only moved. It answers in one line what tracking forces through a changing geometry takes ten to answer.

nodes.name: Momentum
nodes.desc: Mass times velocity, conserved in every collision whether or not energy is. That difference is exactly what separates a bounce from a crash, and it is the reason both are solvable.

nodes.name: Rotation
nodes.desc: Every linear idea again with angles: torque for force, moment of inertia for mass, angular momentum for momentum. The structure repeats exactly, which makes it far less work than it first looks.

nodes.name: Gravitation
nodes.desc: One law covering a dropped apple and a moon, falling off with the square of distance. Orbits are the first case where an object is falling continuously and never arriving.

nodes.name: Fluids
nodes.desc: Pressure, buoyancy and flow. Pressure depending only on depth rather than on the shape of the container is the counterintuitive fact that makes hydraulics work.

nodes.name: Heat & Temperature
nodes.desc: Temperature is how fast the particles jiggle; heat is energy moving because of a temperature difference. Treating them as one thing makes every later result impossible to state properly.

nodes.name: Laws of Thermodynamics
nodes.desc: Energy is conserved, and disorder in a closed system does not decrease. The second law is what forbids perpetual motion and what gives time a direction at all.

nodes.name: Waves
nodes.desc: Energy travelling without matter travelling with it. Frequency, wavelength and speed are locked together, so a wave entering a new medium must change one of them.

nodes.name: Sound & Resonance
nodes.desc: Pressure waves in a medium, and the frequencies at which a system prefers to vibrate. Resonance explains a wine glass shattering and a bridge closing for repairs.

nodes.name: Light & Optics
nodes.desc: Reflection, refraction, lenses and the fact that light bends because it changes speed. Interference is the experiment that ended the argument about whether light is a wave.

nodes.name: Electric Fields
nodes.desc: Charge, and the field describing what a charge would feel at each point. Mathematically the same shape as gravity, with the crucial difference that it can push as well as pull.

nodes.name: Circuits
nodes.desc: Current, voltage and resistance, and the two conservation rules that solve any network of them. Voltage is a difference, and forgetting that is why a bird on a power line is fine.

nodes.name: Magnetism
nodes.desc: Moving charge makes a field, a changing field makes moving charge. That loop is every motor and every generator, and it is what unified electricity and magnetism into one subject.

nodes.name: Electromagnetic Waves
nodes.desc: Fields regenerating each other and propagating at a speed the equations predict outright. That speed turning out to be the speed of light is one of the great results in physics.

nodes.name: Quantum Physics
nodes.desc: Energy arriving in lumps, particles behaving like waves, and outcomes that are probabilities rather than certainties. Strange, exactly right experimentally, and the basis of every semiconductor.

nodes.name: Relativity
nodes.desc: What follows from the speed of light being the same for everybody: time and length stop being absolute. Every satellite fix you use corrects for it, which is as practical as a revolution gets.

nodes.name: States of Matter
nodes.desc: Solid, liquid and gas as three arrangements of the same particles with different energies. Almost every everyday chemical fact is a statement about how tightly particles are held and how fast they move.

nodes.name: Atoms & Elements
nodes.desc: Protons decide what element it is, neutrons decide the isotope, electrons decide the chemistry. Everything else in the subject is a consequence of that last one.

nodes.name: The Periodic Table
nodes.desc: The elements arranged so that a column shares behaviour. It is a prediction machine rather than a reference list: position tells you reactivity, size and what charge an atom is likely to take.

nodes.name: Electron Configuration
nodes.desc: Where electrons sit around a nucleus, in shells and orbitals with room for a fixed number each. The outermost shell being full or nearly full explains why the noble gases do nothing and the halogens do everything.

nodes.name: Bonding
nodes.desc: Atoms sharing or transferring electrons to reach a stable arrangement. Ionic, covalent and metallic are three answers to one question, and which one you get is largely readable off the periodic table.

nodes.name: Molecular Shape
nodes.desc: Electron pairs pushing each other apart, giving molecules definite three-dimensional shapes. Shape decides polarity, polarity decides solubility, and that chain is why water behaves as it does.

nodes.name: The Mole
nodes.desc: A count, like a dozen, chosen so that atomic mass in grams contains one of them. It is the bridge between the mass you can weigh and the number of particles that actually react.

nodes.name: Formulae & Equations
nodes.desc: Writing what reacted and what came out, balanced so no atoms appear or vanish. The balancing is conservation of mass written down, not a puzzle convention.

nodes.name: Stoichiometry
nodes.desc: Using the equation as a recipe: how much of this makes how much of that. Finding the reagent that runs out first is the step that converts a chemical question into an arithmetic one.

nodes.name: Solutions & Concentration
nodes.desc: Dissolving, and saying how much is dissolved per unit of solution. Nearly all reactions you will meet happen in solution, because particles have to meet to react.

nodes.name: Reaction Types
nodes.desc: The handful of patterns most reactions fall into — combination, decomposition, displacement, combustion. Recognising the pattern lets you predict products you have never been taught.

nodes.name: Energy in Reactions
nodes.desc: Breaking bonds costs energy and making them releases it; the difference is what you feel as hot or cold. It also explains why a reaction that releases energy overall still needs a match.

nodes.name: Reaction Rates
nodes.desc: How fast, and the four things that change it: concentration, temperature, surface area and a catalyst. All four work through the same mechanism — how often particles collide hard enough.

nodes.name: Equilibrium
nodes.desc: Reactions that run both ways at once and settle where the two rates match. Nothing has stopped at equilibrium, which is why disturbing it makes the mixture visibly shift to absorb the change.

nodes.name: Acids & Bases
nodes.desc: Donating and accepting protons, measured on a scale where each step is a factor of ten. Buffers resisting change are what keep blood and seawater within the narrow band life needs.

nodes.name: Oxidation & Reduction
nodes.desc: Electrons moving from one species to another, always in pairs of half-reactions. Rusting, respiration and every battery are the same accounting done in different settings.

nodes.name: Electrochemistry
nodes.desc: Driving a redox reaction with electricity or getting electricity out of one. Cells, plating and corrosion protection all fall out of putting the two half-reactions in separate compartments.

nodes.name: Organic Chemistry
nodes.desc: The chemistry of carbon, which bonds four ways and to itself indefinitely. Functional groups are the vocabulary: learn what each one does and a million compounds become a few dozen behaviours.

nodes.name: Laboratory Practice
nodes.desc: Measuring, titrating, purifying and recording it so somebody else could repeat it. Technique is where the uncertainty in a result actually comes from, long before the arithmetic.

nodes.name: Analytical Chemistry
nodes.desc: Working out what a sample actually contains, by spectroscopy, chromatography and titration. Identification and quantification are separate problems, and most real questions need both answered.

nodes.name: What Life Is
nodes.desc: The shared properties of living things: organisation, metabolism, response, reproduction. The borderline cases are the interesting part, which is why a virus is still argued about.

nodes.name: Cells
nodes.desc: The smallest unit that is alive, and the compartments inside it that do separate jobs. Every organism is one of these or a colony of them cooperating.

nodes.name: Membranes & Transport
nodes.desc: A boundary that decides what gets in and out, some of it for free and some at a cost. Osmosis is the case worth being fluent in, because it explains wilting, swelling and why saltwater dehydrates you.

nodes.name: Biological Molecules
nodes.desc: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids — four families doing nearly everything. Structure predicts function throughout, which is why a change to one amino acid can break an entire organism.

nodes.name: Enzymes
nodes.desc: Proteins that make a specific reaction fast enough to be useful at body temperature. Their shape is the whole mechanism, which is why heat and the wrong acidity destroy them permanently.

nodes.name: Respiration
nodes.desc: Releasing energy from food into a form a cell can spend. The aerobic route yields far more than the anaerobic one, which is exactly why muscles burn when the oxygen runs short.

nodes.name: Photosynthesis
nodes.desc: Building sugar out of air and water using light. Nearly every calorie in every food chain entered biology through this reaction, which makes it the most important one on the planet.

nodes.name: DNA
nodes.desc: A four-letter code that stores instructions and copies itself accurately. The pairing rule is the whole trick: each strand carries enough information to rebuild the other.

nodes.name: Protein Synthesis
nodes.desc: Copying a gene and translating it three letters at a time into a chain of amino acids. This is where a sequence stops being information and starts being a working machine.

nodes.name: Cell Division
nodes.desc: One cell becoming two identical ones for growth, or four half-loaded ones for reproduction. The second kind shuffles the deck, which is where most of the variation in a population comes from.

nodes.name: Genetics
nodes.desc: How traits pass down, and why an unexpressed variant can reappear generations later. The simple dominant and recessive cases are the exception; most traits are many genes and an environment.

nodes.name: Mutation & Variation
nodes.desc: Copying errors and damage, most of which do nothing and some of which change a protein. Variation is not a defect in the system; without it a population cannot respond to anything.

nodes.name: Evolution
nodes.desc: Heritable variation plus differential survival, repeated. It requires no foresight and no goal, which is the part that is genuinely hard to hold onto while reading about adaptation.

nodes.name: Classification
nodes.desc: Grouping organisms by shared ancestry rather than by resemblance. Convergence is why a dolphin and a shark look alike and sit nowhere near each other on the tree.

nodes.name: Organ Systems
nodes.desc: Cells into tissues into organs into systems, each solving a problem that a single cell solves by diffusion alone. Size is the reason multicellular life needs any of this machinery.

nodes.name: Homeostasis
nodes.desc: Holding internal conditions steady while the outside moves, by negative feedback. Temperature, blood sugar and water balance are three instances of one control pattern.

nodes.name: Nerves & Hormones
nodes.desc: Two signalling systems: one electrical and fast down a fixed wire, one chemical and slow but reaching everywhere. Which one a body uses for a job is decided by how quickly the answer is needed.

nodes.name: Immunity
nodes.desc: Distinguishing self from not-self, and remembering an intruder well enough to answer faster next time. Vaccination is that memory installed without the illness that would normally create it.

nodes.name: Ecology
nodes.desc: Organisms interacting with each other and with the physical world. Energy flows through and is lost at each step; matter cycles round, which is why food chains are short and nutrients are not.

nodes.name: Populations
nodes.desc: Growth, limits and the interactions that hold numbers where they are. Exponential growth meeting a ceiling is the model behind conservation, epidemics and pest control alike.

nodes.name: Biotechnology
nodes.desc: Reading, editing and building with the same molecules. The techniques are now routine enough that the interesting constraints are ethical and ecological rather than technical.

nodes.name: Deep Time
nodes.desc: Getting used to spans where a millimetre a year builds a mountain range. Almost every argument against these subjects is really a failure to take four billion years seriously as a number.

nodes.name: Rocks & Minerals
nodes.desc: Three families defined by how they formed: cooled, compressed or transformed. Identifying which one you are holding tells you what was happening where it was made.

nodes.name: Inside the Earth
nodes.desc: Crust, mantle and core, deduced almost entirely from how earthquake waves bend on their way through. Nobody has drilled past the crust, and we still know the structure with confidence.

nodes.name: Plate Tectonics
nodes.desc: A cracked shell moving on a slow-flowing interior. It is the one theory that explains mountains, earthquakes, volcanoes and matching fossils on opposite coasts at the same time.

nodes.name: Earthquakes & Volcanoes
nodes.desc: What happens at the edges where plates meet, and why the hazard maps look the way they do. The magnitude scale is logarithmic, so two steps up is a thousand times the energy.

nodes.name: Reading the Record
nodes.desc: Layers, fossils and radiometric dating as three independent clocks that agree. Their agreement is the evidence, far more than any one of them alone.

nodes.name: Weather
nodes.desc: Uneven heating, moving air and water changing state. Fronts, pressure and humidity between them account for nearly everything a forecast is trying to say.

nodes.name: The Atmosphere
nodes.desc: A thin layered envelope held on by gravity, with almost all the weather in the bottom slice. Its composition is what keeps the surface habitable and what makes changing it consequential.

nodes.name: Oceans & Currents
nodes.desc: A heat store that moves energy around the planet on a conveyor driven by temperature and salt. It is why one coast at a given latitude is temperate and another is not.

nodes.name: Earth Cycles
nodes.desc: Water, carbon, nitrogen and rock, each moving through reservoirs on wildly different timescales. Understanding where a cycle stores things and for how long is what makes any of it predictable.

nodes.name: Climate
nodes.desc: The statistics of weather over decades, and the balance between energy arriving and leaving. Feedbacks are the part that matters: ice reflecting sunlight it no longer reflects once it melts.

nodes.name: Resources & Hazards
nodes.desc: Where useful materials concentrate, and where living is dangerous. Both answers come from the same processes, which is why the most fertile ground is often at the foot of a volcano.

nodes.name: The Sky
nodes.desc: What moves, how often and why, from a fixed spot on a spinning tilted planet. Seasons come from the tilt rather than the distance, which is the most commonly held wrong belief in the subject.

nodes.name: The Solar System
nodes.desc: A star, eight planets and an enormous amount of empty space drawn to scale by almost nobody. Orbits, moons and the division between rocky and gas worlds all trace back to how it formed.

nodes.name: Orbits & Gravity
nodes.desc: Continuous falling that keeps missing the ground. Once that clicks, tides, satellites and why astronauts float all stop being separate facts.

nodes.name: Light from Space
nodes.desc: Almost everything known about the universe arrived as light. Splitting it reveals composition, temperature and motion, which is how a chemical analysis of a star is possible at all.

nodes.name: Stars
nodes.desc: Fusion holding gravity off for billions of years, then losing. How a star dies depends almost entirely on its mass, and the heavy elements you are made of came from those deaths.

nodes.name: Galaxies
nodes.desc: Hundreds of billions of stars bound together, rotating faster at the edges than the visible mass allows. That discrepancy is the observation that put dark matter on the table.

nodes.name: Cosmology
nodes.desc: The universe as one object with a history: expanding, cooling, and leaving a faint glow behind. Distant galaxies receding faster the further away they are is the observation the whole picture rests on.

nodes.name: Observation & Instruments
nodes.desc: Telescopes, satellites, cores and seismographs — evidence gathered where an experiment is impossible. Every one of these subjects advances by finding a new thing to measure rather than a new thing to try.

nodes.name: Earth as a System
nodes.desc: Rock, air, water and life as four coupled parts that have shaped each other for billions of years. Oxygen in the atmosphere is biological in origin, which is the clearest case of the coupling running both ways.

nodes.name: Reading the Question
nodes.desc: Working out what is being asked and what has quietly been given, before any formula is written down. Olympiad problems hide the given quantity in a clause, and the reach for an equation is what walks past it.

nodes.name: Units & Estimation
nodes.desc: Carrying units through an expression so a wrong one announces itself, and knowing the order of magnitude before computing. On a multiple-choice paper the estimate frequently is the answer.

nodes.name: Uncertainty
nodes.desc: How error in a measurement propagates into everything computed from it, and how many figures you are entitled to report. The lab events grade this directly and the written papers assume it.

nodes.name: Free-Body Diagrams
nodes.desc: Every force on one object and nothing else on the page. Almost every mechanics mistake at this level is a force drawn that was not acting, or one acting that was not drawn.

nodes.name: Stoichiometry
nodes.desc: Counting particles by weighing them, and the ratio a balanced equation actually asserts. The limiting reagent is where this is tested, because it is where the arithmetic stops being proportional.

nodes.name: Cell Biology
nodes.desc: Membranes, organelles and the reactions that pay for everything a cell does. Olympiad biology assumes this the way olympiad physics assumes algebra — as vocabulary rather than as content.

nodes.name: Kinematics & Dynamics
nodes.desc: Position, velocity and acceleration as one another’s derivatives, and Newton’s laws applied to a diagram you drew correctly. Choosing the axes well is worth more than any algebraic technique here.

nodes.name: Energy & Momentum
nodes.desc: Conservation laws, and knowing which one survives a given collision. They turn problems that are brutal in forces into two lines of arithmetic, which is exactly why the paper is written to obscure that they apply.

nodes.name: Chemical Equilibrium
nodes.desc: Reactions that arrive somewhere and stop, and what shifts them. Le Chatelier gives the direction in a sentence; the equilibrium constant is what makes it a number.

nodes.name: Redox & Electrochemistry
nodes.desc: Tracking electrons through a reaction and the voltage that transfer is worth. Balancing a half-reaction in acid is mechanical, heavily examined, and dropped by people who never practised it under time.

nodes.name: Genetics
nodes.desc: Inheritance as probability, from a cross through linkage to population frequencies. The pedigree questions are logic puzzles wearing a lab coat, which is why they reward practice rather than reading.

nodes.name: Physiology
nodes.desc: Systems that hold a body at a set point, and what the feedback loop does when it is pushed. Homeostasis is the through-line, and an answer that does not name a feedback mechanism is usually incomplete.

nodes.name: The F=ma Exam
nodes.desc: Twenty-five mechanics problems in seventy-five minutes with no calculator, which makes it a test of setup speed rather than of depth. The estimate and the free-body diagram between them decide most of the score.

nodes.name: Thermodynamics
nodes.desc: Energy, entropy and which direction a process will go on its own. It is the one topic both the physics and the chemistry ladders examine, from opposite ends and with different notation.

nodes.name: Ecology & Evolution
nodes.desc: Populations changing over time, under selection and under each other. The quantitative half — Hardy-Weinberg, growth models — is what the olympiad rounds actually test.

nodes.name: The Lab Practical
nodes.desc: Doing the measurement, recording it honestly, and writing the uncertainty beside it under a time limit. Graded on the notebook as much as the number, which is a shock to people who only ever sat written papers.

nodes.name: Electricity & Magnetism
nodes.desc: Fields, potential and the fact that a changing one of each makes the other. The second semester exam assumes calculus fluency in a way the mechanics paper does not.

nodes.name: Chemistry Olympiad
nodes.desc: A national exam with a laboratory part, where the written half rewards breadth and the practical half rewards having actually handled glassware. Very few competitors are strong at both.

nodes.name: Biology Olympiad
nodes.desc: The broadest syllabus of the three by a distance, examined at a depth textbooks do not reach. Semifinalists are separated by reading primary literature rather than by revising harder.

nodes.name: Modern Physics
nodes.desc: Relativity and quantisation, where the classical answer is confidently wrong. It appears late in the selection ladder and rewards understanding the postulates over memorising the results.

nodes.name: Selection Camp
nodes.desc: The round after the national exam, where problems take hours rather than minutes and a partial argument is worth writing. Everything below converges here because nothing at this level announces its topic.

nodes.name: Reading Fluently
nodes.desc: Getting through a page without decoding it word by word, so attention is free for the meaning. Everything else in this tree assumes it, and it is built by volume rather than by exercises.

nodes.name: Vocabulary
nodes.desc: Words known well enough to use, not merely to recognise. Learning them inside a sentence you met them in beats a list, because the connotation is most of what a word actually carries.

nodes.name: Spelling & Sound
nodes.desc: The patterns behind English spelling, which is far more regular than its reputation once you know where the borrowings came from. Knowing the pattern beats memorising the exception.

nodes.name: Parts of Speech
nodes.desc: What each word is doing in a sentence rather than what it means. It is the vocabulary you need to talk about why a sentence is broken instead of only feeling that it is.

nodes.name: Sentences
nodes.desc: Subject, verb and the clauses hanging off them. Most bad writing is not a vocabulary problem; it is sentences with too many things going on and no clear main action.

nodes.name: Punctuation
nodes.desc: Marks that show a reader how the parts fit together. The comma splice and the misused apostrophe are the two errors that cost credibility fastest, and both take an afternoon to fix for good.

nodes.name: Tense & Agreement
nodes.desc: Keeping time consistent and making the parts of a sentence match. Drifting between past and present mid-paragraph is invisible while writing and glaring on the second read.

nodes.name: Paragraphs
nodes.desc: One idea, developed, with a sentence that says what it is. A paragraph that changes subject halfway is two paragraphs, and splitting them is the cheapest structural improvement there is.

nodes.name: Summarising
nodes.desc: Saying in three sentences what took three pages, without smuggling in your own view. It is the most reliable test of whether something was actually understood.

nodes.name: Note-Taking
nodes.desc: Capturing meaning rather than transcribing words, in a form your later self can use. Notes that are shorter than the source and rewritten in your own phrasing are the ones that survive.

nodes.name: Close Reading
nodes.desc: Reading for how something is said as well as what it says: word choice, structure, what is left out. It is the difference between having an opinion about a text and having evidence.

nodes.name: Argument
nodes.desc: A claim, reasons and the evidence under them, arranged so a sceptical reader follows. Anticipating the strongest objection rather than the weakest is what separates persuasion from assertion.

nodes.name: Tone & Register
nodes.desc: Matching how formal, warm or direct the writing is to who is reading it. The same content in the wrong register reads as rude, unserious or evasive, none of which was meant.

nodes.name: Editing
nodes.desc: Cutting, reordering and tightening after the draft exists. Nearly every first draft loses a fifth of its words with no loss of meaning, and finding them is a separate sitting from writing them.

nodes.name: Research & Sources
nodes.desc: Finding material, judging whether it is any good, and tracking where each fact came from. Recording the source at the moment you use it costs seconds and saves an evening.

nodes.name: Citation & Integrity
nodes.desc: Attributing ideas and quotations in a consistent style. The rule underneath the formatting is simple: a reader should always be able to tell which thoughts are yours.

nodes.name: Speaking & Discussion
nodes.desc: Making a point aloud, listening to the reply, and changing your mind in public when it is warranted. Structure helps more than confidence: one claim, one reason, one example.

nodes.name: Listening
nodes.desc: Following an argument you did not construct, including the part you disagree with. Being able to restate a position you disagree with, to the satisfaction of the person holding it, to their satisfaction is the test worth applying.

nodes.name: Style
nodes.desc: The choices that make prose yours: rhythm, sentence length, how much you leave to the reader. It arrives from reading widely and imitating deliberately, not from adjectives.

nodes.name: A Writing Habit
nodes.desc: Words on a schedule rather than when inspired. Every professional writer describes the same discovery: the sitting down produces the ideas, not the other way round.

nodes.name: Drafting
nodes.desc: Writing badly on purpose to get something to work with. Editing while drafting is the most common way a piece takes four times as long and comes out worse.

nodes.name: Audience & Purpose
nodes.desc: Who reads this and what they should be able to do afterwards. Almost every question about tone, length and how much to explain answers itself once those two are written down.

nodes.name: Outlining
nodes.desc: Deciding the order before committing sentences to it. Even a five-line outline prevents the commonest structural failure, which is a piece that arrives at its point in the last paragraph.

nodes.name: The Central Claim
nodes.desc: The one sentence the whole piece is defending. If it cannot be written in one sentence, the piece is not ready to be written, however much research is behind it.

nodes.name: Openings
nodes.desc: Earning the second paragraph. Written last, almost always, because you do not know what you were introducing until the piece exists.

nodes.name: Flow & Transitions
nodes.desc: Each paragraph picking up something the last one put down. When writing feels choppy the cause is usually order rather than sentence quality.

nodes.name: Clarity
nodes.desc: Making the subject do the action and putting the important thing at the end of the sentence. Two habits that fix more prose than any amount of vocabulary.

nodes.name: Concision
nodes.desc: Removing words that are doing nothing. It is a mechanical pass rather than a talent, and it is the fastest visible improvement any writer makes.

nodes.name: Revision
nodes.desc: Rewriting at the level of structure, not commas. That means being willing to cut a section you like, which is why it is easier a day later than an hour later.

nodes.name: Taking Feedback
nodes.desc: Hearing where a reader got lost without arguing that they should not have. Readers are reliable about where the problem is and unreliable about what would fix it.

nodes.name: Essays
nodes.desc: An argument built in public, with the evidence shown. The form rewards conceding the strongest counter-argument early rather than pretending it does not exist.

nodes.name: Reports & Documentation
nodes.desc: Writing that people navigate rather than read: headings, summaries and a structure that survives being skimmed. The conclusion goes first, which reverses everything essay writing taught.

nodes.name: Professional Writing
nodes.desc: Emails and messages that get a decision instead of a thread. Ask for one thing, say when it is needed, and put both in the first two lines.

nodes.name: Narrative
nodes.desc: Somebody wanting something and having trouble getting it. Scene by scene, with tension that changes rather than repeats, is most of what makes a story readable.

nodes.name: Character & Dialogue
nodes.desc: People who want incompatible things, talking past each other. Dialogue that only exchanges information is the most common thing that makes fiction feel flat.

nodes.name: Description & Image
nodes.desc: One precise detail rather than three vague ones. The rule that outlives every workshop is to give the reader something to see and let them supply the adjective.

nodes.name: Poetry
nodes.desc: Compression, line breaks and sound doing work that sentences alone cannot. Reading it aloud is not optional; the ear catches what the eye forgives.

nodes.name: Long-Form Projects
nodes.desc: Holding something together across months, when momentum matters more than any single day. Finishing badly and revising beats stalling in pursuit of a perfect chapter three.

nodes.name: Voice
nodes.desc: Writing that could not be by anybody else. It comes from imitating deliberately until the imitations stop fitting, rather than from trying to be original at the start.

nodes.name: Publishing
nodes.desc: Submitting, being rejected, and sending it out again the same week. The manuscript is half the work; the other half is the unglamorous business of putting it in front of people.

nodes.name: Reading Widely
nodes.desc: Enough books, across enough kinds, that comparisons become available. Every later skill here is a way of noticing, and noticing needs something to notice against.

nodes.name: Plot & Structure
nodes.desc: What happens, in what order, and why that order. Noticing where a book withholds information is the first step from summarising a story to reading one.

nodes.name: Character
nodes.desc: People built from what they want, what they do about it, and what they say instead. A character who changes is the engine of most fiction, and the change is usually smaller than the plot.

nodes.name: Narrator & Point of View
nodes.desc: Who is telling this, how much they know, and whether they can be trusted. Recognising an unreliable narrator changes everything a book appeared to be saying.

nodes.name: Setting & Atmosphere
nodes.desc: Where and when, and what that does to what is possible. Setting is rarely decoration; it is usually the constraint the whole conflict depends on.

nodes.name: Imagery & Figurative Language
nodes.desc: Metaphor, simile and the images a book keeps returning to. A repeated image is a claim the book is making without stating it.

nodes.name: Theme
nodes.desc: What the book is about underneath what happens in it. A theme is an argument rather than a topic, which is why "love" is not one and "what love costs" might be.

nodes.name: Form & Genre
nodes.desc: The conventions a work is written inside, and what breaking one signals. Genre is a set of expectations shared with the reader, and the interesting books know exactly which one they are refusing.

nodes.name: Reading Poetry
nodes.desc: Line, sound, compression and what the break at the end of a line does to a phrase. Read aloud twice before deciding what it means, and expect the first reading to be wrong.

nodes.name: Reading Drama
nodes.desc: Text written to be performed, where nobody narrates and everything must be shown or said. What a character conceals is doing as much work as what they announce.

nodes.name: Close Reading
nodes.desc: Building a reading of a whole work out of a paragraph of it. The discipline is that every claim points at specific words, which is what makes it an argument rather than an impression.

nodes.name: Historical Context
nodes.desc: What the book was answering, and what its first readers took for granted. Context explains choices that look like flaws from here and stops anachronistic readings.

nodes.name: Movements & Tradition
nodes.desc: The conversations books have with each other across centuries. Most famous works are replies, and knowing what they are replying to is half the meaning.

nodes.name: Comparative Reading
nodes.desc: Two texts side by side, chosen so the comparison produces something neither would alone. The pairing is the argument, and a lazy pairing cannot be rescued by good analysis.

nodes.name: Critical Approaches
nodes.desc: Deliberate lenses — historical, psychological, political, formal — each making some features visible and others invisible. The point is choosing one knowingly rather than having one by default.

nodes.name: The Literary Essay
nodes.desc: A claim about a text, defended with quotation and analysis rather than plot summary. The commonest failure is retelling the book to a reader who has read it.

nodes.name: Literature in Translation
nodes.desc: Reading work whose sentences somebody else chose. Comparing two translations of one paragraph is the fastest lesson in how much of style is decision.

nodes.name: Canon & Its Critics
nodes.desc: How a set of books came to be the set everybody studies, and who decided. The argument about what was left out is itself one of the more interesting things in the subject.

nodes.name: Literary Research
nodes.desc: Finding what has already been argued, and locating the gap your reading fills. Knowing the existing scholarship is what turns an opinion into a contribution.

nodes.name: Your Own Reading
nodes.desc: An interpretation you can defend that is genuinely yours, held loosely enough to revise. That is the whole point of the apparatus, and it is easy to lose sight of behind the apparatus.

nodes.name: Sounds & Script
nodes.desc: The sounds the language uses and the marks it writes them with, learned before any vocabulary. A word learned with the wrong sounds has to be unlearned, and that is far more expensive than a slow start.

nodes.name: Core Vocabulary
nodes.desc: The first thousand words, which cover most of ordinary speech. Frequency order is not a preference here; it is the difference between six months and three years to a first conversation.

nodes.name: Survival Phrases
nodes.desc: Greetings, asking for things, and the sentences that keep a conversation alive when you are lost. "Say that again slowly" is worth more than fifty nouns.

nodes.name: Basic Grammar
nodes.desc: Word order, and how verbs change for who is doing what and when. Enough structure to build sentences you have never heard, which is the point at which phrases become a language.

nodes.name: Listening
nodes.desc: Making out words in speech at full speed, where they run together and nothing is enunciated. It lags behind reading for everybody, and the only fix is hours of it.

nodes.name: Speaking
nodes.desc: Producing sentences aloud, badly, in front of somebody. The willingness to be wrong out loud is the single largest predictor of how fast anybody learns a language.

nodes.name: Reading
nodes.desc: Text you can work through with a dictionary, then text you can follow without one. Graded material first: reading something too hard teaches vocabulary and destroys the habit.

nodes.name: Tenses & Aspect
nodes.desc: Talking about what happened, what will, and what was ongoing when something else interrupted. Languages divide time differently, and the divisions rarely map onto the ones you grew up with.

nodes.name: Cases & Agreement
nodes.desc: How a language marks who did what to whom — endings, particles, or strict word order. Whichever system it uses, it is doing a job your first language does some other way.

nodes.name: Comprehensible Input
nodes.desc: Large amounts of material just above your level, understood mostly from context. This is where most real acquisition happens, and it does not feel like studying, which is why it gets skipped.

nodes.name: Spaced Review
nodes.desc: Reviewing each item just before you would forget it. Twenty minutes daily beats three hours weekly by a wide margin, and cards made from sentences you met beat cards bought in a deck.

nodes.name: Conversation
nodes.desc: Real exchanges at real speed, including the part where you did not catch it. Learning to repair a conversation without switching to English is a skill of its own.

nodes.name: Writing
nodes.desc: Producing text with time to think, which exposes exactly the gaps speaking lets you skate over. Getting a sentence corrected teaches more than getting a paragraph praised.

nodes.name: Idiom & Collocation
nodes.desc: Which words go together, which is mostly arbitrary and entirely noticeable. Grammatically perfect sentences that no native speaker would say are the last thing to disappear.

nodes.name: Register & Politeness
nodes.desc: Formal and casual, and who gets which. Some languages encode it in the verb itself, and getting it wrong reads as rudeness rather than as a learner error.

nodes.name: Cultural Context
nodes.desc: What is assumed, what is impolite to say directly, and the references everybody shares. Language separated from this produces sentences that are correct and land wrongly.

nodes.name: Native Media
nodes.desc: Film, news and books made for native speakers rather than for you. The first ones are exhausting; the transition from subtitles to none is the milestone most learners remember.

nodes.name: Fluency
nodes.desc: Speaking without translating in your head, and thinking in the language for stretches. It arrives gradually and is usually noticed in retrospect, often by somebody else.

nodes.name: Translating
nodes.desc: Carrying meaning across rather than words, and deciding what to lose. Being fluent in both languages is a prerequisite and nowhere near sufficient.

nodes.name: Maintenance
nodes.desc: Keeping a language you stopped studying. Without regular contact it fades faster than anything else you have learned, and reading twenty minutes a week holds most of it.

nodes.name: Asking a Question
nodes.desc: Turning an interest into something that could actually be answered with evidence. "Was the revolution inevitable" is a topic; "what did the people who joined it say they wanted" is a question.

nodes.name: Sources
nodes.desc: Primary material made at the time, and secondary work written about it afterwards. Knowing which you are holding decides what it can be used to prove.

nodes.name: Source Criticism
nodes.desc: Who made this, for whom, and what they wanted the reader to believe. A biased source is not a useless source; it is excellent evidence about the person who produced it.

nodes.name: Evidence & Inference
nodes.desc: The gap between what a document shows and what you want to conclude, crossed explicitly. Most weak arguments in these subjects are a hidden step in that crossing.

nodes.name: Context
nodes.desc: What was normal, sayable and possible at the time. Judging a decision by what everybody knows now is the error that makes the past look stupid rather than different.

nodes.name: Bias & Perspective
nodes.desc: Every account is from somewhere, including yours. The useful move is naming the position rather than hunting for a source that has none, because there are none.

nodes.name: Constructing an Argument
nodes.desc: A claim, the evidence, and why the evidence supports that claim rather than another. Handling the counter-example directly is what makes an argument stand up.

nodes.name: Reasoning & Fallacies
nodes.desc: The common ways an argument fails while sounding fine. Naming a fallacy is not a refutation on its own, and treating it as one is itself a habit worth losing.

nodes.name: Comparison
nodes.desc: Putting two cases side by side so the differences say something. Choosing cases that are similar enough for the difference to mean anything is most of the work.

nodes.name: Continuity & Change
nodes.desc: What actually shifted, how fast, and what stayed the same underneath. Periods are labels applied afterwards, and people living through them rarely noticed the boundary.

nodes.name: Cause & Consequence
nodes.desc: Distinguishing what made something possible, what made it likely, and what set it off. Single-cause explanations of large events are almost always a shortened version of a real argument.

nodes.name: People & Societies
nodes.desc: Groups, institutions and the rules that hold them together. Sociology as a habit rather than a subject: asking what a structure is doing rather than only what a person decided.

nodes.name: Place & Geography
nodes.desc: Rivers, mountains, distance and climate as constraints on what people could do. It is not determinism to notice that the map made some outcomes much cheaper than others.

nodes.name: Power & Politics
nodes.desc: Who decides, how they keep the ability to decide, and who is excluded. Formal institutions are half of it; the informal half is where most of it actually happens.

nodes.name: Economy & Society
nodes.desc: How people made a living, and what that allowed and prevented. Following the material constraints explains a surprising amount of what looks like pure ideology.

nodes.name: History of Ideas
nodes.desc: Where beliefs came from and what they were reacting against. Most ideas that feel obvious now were once a minority position with a specific opponent in mind.

nodes.name: Writing in the Humanities
nodes.desc: An essay that advances a position and shows its evidence, rather than surveying what others said. The literature review is background; the argument is the piece.

nodes.name: Ethical Reasoning
nodes.desc: Working out what should be done, with reasons somebody who disagrees can engage with. It is a discipline rather than an opinion, and the disagreements are usually about which principle wins.

nodes.name: Chronology
nodes.desc: A rough frame of what came before what, across more than one part of the world. Not an end in itself, and impossible to argue about causes without it.

nodes.name: Periods & Labels
nodes.desc: Ancient, medieval, modern and the rest are conveniences invented afterwards. Knowing they are arguments rather than facts is what stops them quietly doing your thinking.

nodes.name: Working with Sources
nodes.desc: Documents, objects, images and testimony, and what survived by accident rather than by importance. Absence of evidence is usually a fact about record-keeping rather than about the past.

nodes.name: Dating & Evidence
nodes.desc: Working out when something happened when nobody wrote it down: layers, materials, cross-references, radiocarbon. Independent methods agreeing is what turns a guess into a date.

nodes.name: Building a Narrative
nodes.desc: Turning fragments into an account, and being honest about the joins. Every narrative chooses a start point, and the choice is already an argument about causes.

nodes.name: Social History
nodes.desc: Ordinary lives: work, food, family, illness. Harder to research because ordinary people left fewer documents, and the part that changes how the period actually felt.

nodes.name: Political History
nodes.desc: States, rulers, laws and wars — the traditional spine of the subject. Best read as one thread among several rather than the frame everything else fits into.

nodes.name: Economic History
nodes.desc: Trade, prices, harvests and who owned the land. Long series of dull numbers explain more political upheaval than most political documents do.

nodes.name: Cultural History
nodes.desc: Belief, ritual, art and what people found funny or shameful. It is the fastest route to the fact that the past was genuinely foreign rather than us in worse clothes.

nodes.name: Empires & Encounter
nodes.desc: Expansion, conquest and what happened where two societies met. The sources are overwhelmingly from one side, and reading against them is a technique in itself.

nodes.name: Revolutions
nodes.desc: Moments when the arrangement of power broke rather than bent. They look inevitable afterwards and looked impossible a year before, which is the thing worth explaining.

nodes.name: War & Its Aftermath
nodes.desc: Causes, conduct and the settlements that set up the next one. Battles are the least explanatory part; logistics, finance and what happened afterwards do most of the work.

nodes.name: Technology & Change
nodes.desc: Printing, steam, rail, antibiotics and the internet — inventions that reorganised what was possible. Adoption is usually slower and stranger than the invention story suggests.

nodes.name: Global Connections
nodes.desc: Following goods, diseases, people and ideas across borders instead of inside them. Many national histories stop making sense the moment you look at the shipping.

nodes.name: Memory & Commemoration
nodes.desc: How a society remembers, forgets and argues about its own past. What gets a statue is evidence about the people who put it up rather than about the person on it.

nodes.name: Quantitative History
nodes.desc: Censuses, tax rolls and parish records treated as data. It answers questions no chronicle can and inherits every bias in who was counted.

nodes.name: Oral History
nodes.desc: Testimony gathered from people who were there, decades later. Memory reshapes itself over time, and that reshaping is itself a subject rather than only a limitation.

nodes.name: Public History
nodes.desc: History outside the academy: museums, documentaries, curricula and heritage. What the public believes about the past is decided here far more than in journals.

nodes.name: Historiography
nodes.desc: The history of the writing of history: what each generation thought worth explaining and what it could not see. Reading it makes the current consensus visible as a position rather than as the truth.

nodes.name: Doing Research
nodes.desc: A question, an archive, months of material that answers something else, and an argument at the end. The gap between reading history and producing it is mostly patience.

nodes.name: Arguments
nodes.desc: Premises, a conclusion, and the claim that the second follows from the first. Separating whether the reasoning is valid from whether the premises are true is the first move and the one people skip.

nodes.name: Formal Logic
nodes.desc: Rules of inference that hold regardless of subject matter. Symbolising an argument strips the rhetoric off it and shows what was actually being claimed.

nodes.name: Fallacies
nodes.desc: Standard ways of reasoning badly while sounding persuasive. Useful for reading your own drafts, and overused as a way of dismissing arguments without answering them.

nodes.name: Concepts & Definitions
nodes.desc: Being precise about what a word is being used to mean here. A surprising number of long disagreements dissolve the moment both sides define the central term.

nodes.name: Thought Experiments
nodes.desc: Impossible cases built to isolate one intuition. They are instruments rather than stories, and complaining that the scenario is unrealistic usually misses what it is for.

nodes.name: Epistemology
nodes.desc: What knowledge is and when a belief is justified. Scepticism is not the answer here; it is the pressure test every account of knowledge has to survive.

nodes.name: Metaphysics
nodes.desc: What exists and what kind of thing it is: objects, properties, time, identity over change. Abstract until it turns out that most disputes elsewhere depend on an answer here.

nodes.name: Philosophy of Mind
nodes.desc: How thought relates to matter, and what conscious experience even is. The hard question is not how brains process information but why any of it is like something from the inside.

nodes.name: Free Will
nodes.desc: Whether choices could have been otherwise, and whether it matters for responsibility. Most of the interesting work argues that determinism and responsibility are compatible, which is less obvious than either extreme.

nodes.name: Ethics
nodes.desc: What makes an action right — consequences, duties, or the character it expresses. The three main answers each get some cases obviously right and one case famously wrong.

nodes.name: Applied Ethics
nodes.desc: Medicine, animals, war, technology and the environment, argued case by case. It is where the theories earn their keep or turn out to be unusable.

nodes.name: Political Philosophy
nodes.desc: What makes authority legitimate and what a just distribution would look like. Every actual political argument is standing on an unstated answer to one of these.

nodes.name: Aesthetics
nodes.desc: What art is, and whether a judgement of beauty claims anything beyond a preference. The interesting cases are the ones where taste feels like it should be arguable.

nodes.name: Philosophy of Science
nodes.desc: What makes a claim scientific, how theories are chosen, and what happens when one is overturned. It takes the method seriously enough to ask what it actually guarantees.

nodes.name: Philosophy of Language
nodes.desc: How words attach to things, and how a sentence gets to be about anything at all. A great deal of twentieth-century philosophy runs through this question.

nodes.name: Ancient Philosophy
nodes.desc: The Greek beginnings, where the questions were set and several answers still stand. Reading the dialogues is also the best available demonstration of what an argument in good faith looks like.

nodes.name: Modern Philosophy
nodes.desc: The turn to the knowing subject: rationalists, empiricists, and the synthesis that tried to end the argument. Most contemporary debates are still using vocabulary settled here.

nodes.name: Contemporary Traditions
nodes.desc: The split into analytic and continental approaches, and the traditions outside Europe that were doing this all along. Knowing what each is trying to achieve makes the mutual dismissals less confusing.

nodes.name: Writing Philosophy
nodes.desc: One claim, defended, with the strongest objection answered rather than avoided. Clarity is the whole style: obscurity in this subject is nearly always a sign the thought is not finished.

nodes.name: The Examined Life
nodes.desc: Actually applying any of it to how you live and what you believe. The subject is famously capable of being studied for years with no such contact, which was never the intention.

nodes.name: Research Methods
nodes.desc: Experiments, observation and self-report, and what each can and cannot establish. Almost every disagreement in the field is really about whether the design supports the claim.

nodes.name: Measuring the Mind
nodes.desc: Turning something internal into a number: reaction times, scales, physiological signals. Validity is the whole question — whether the thing you measured is the thing you meant.

nodes.name: Statistics in Psychology
nodes.desc: Effect sizes, confidence and the difference between significant and important. A field studying small effects in noisy samples has to be unusually careful here, and historically was not.

nodes.name: Replication
nodes.desc: Whether a result appears again when somebody else runs it. A large fraction of famous findings did not, and knowing which is now part of basic literacy in the subject.

nodes.name: Research Ethics
nodes.desc: Consent, deception, debriefing and the right to withdraw. The rules exist because several of the most cited studies of the last century would not be approved today.

nodes.name: Brain & Behaviour
nodes.desc: Which structures do what, and the limits of inferring a mental process from a bright patch on a scan. Localisation is real and far less tidy than popular accounts suggest.

nodes.name: Perception
nodes.desc: Sensation arriving and being turned into an experience of a world. Illusions are the standard tool because they show the construction happening rather than a fault in it.

nodes.name: Attention
nodes.desc: What gets processed out of everything arriving, and what does not. The reliable finding is that people miss far more than they believe they do, including in plain sight.

nodes.name: Memory
nodes.desc: Encoding, storing and reconstructing — and it is genuinely reconstruction. Confident memories can be entirely false, which is a fact with consequences well outside the laboratory.

nodes.name: Learning
nodes.desc: Conditioning, reinforcement and how practice changes behaviour. Spacing and retrieval beat repetition and rereading, which is one of the best-replicated results in the field.

nodes.name: Thinking & Reasoning
nodes.desc: Problem solving, judgement and the shortcuts that usually work. Biases are not stupidity; they are heuristics being applied outside the conditions they were good for.

nodes.name: Language & Thought
nodes.desc: How language is acquired so fast, and how much it shapes what can be thought. The strong version of that second claim has not survived; the weak version keeps producing results.

nodes.name: Development
nodes.desc: How thinking, attachment and moral reasoning change from infancy onward. Stage theories are useful frames and less rigid than their diagrams imply.

nodes.name: Social Psychology
nodes.desc: How the presence of others changes what people do. Situation beats disposition far more often than intuition allows, and that finding survived the replication crisis better than most.

nodes.name: Personality
nodes.desc: Stable differences between people, and the five dimensions that keep reappearing across cultures. Popular type indicators are not among the things that replicated.

nodes.name: Emotion & Motivation
nodes.desc: What emotions are for, how they are regulated, and why people persist at some things and not others. Reward that undermines existing interest is the finding worth knowing first.

nodes.name: Clinical Psychology
nodes.desc: How disorders are classified, and what the evidence says about treating them. Diagnosis is a working description rather than a discovered category, and the manual is revised for exactly that reason.

nodes.name: Health & Stress
nodes.desc: The routes between mind and body: stress, sleep, pain and adherence. Chronic activation of a system built for short emergencies explains a large share of it.

nodes.name: Applied Psychology
nodes.desc: Psychology in workplaces, classrooms, courts and interfaces. It is also where findings get oversold, so the method nodes at the top of this tree stay relevant.

nodes.name: Reading the Literature
nodes.desc: Reading a paper for its sample, its design and its analysis before its abstract. The whole tree points here: being able to tell a solid finding from a well-publicised one.

nodes.name: Claim, Warrant, Impact
nodes.desc: What you say, why it is true, and why anybody should care. An argument missing the warrant is an assertion and an argument missing the impact is trivia, and judges discount both without saying so.

nodes.name: Speaking Clearly
nodes.desc: Being understood at whatever rate you have chosen, with the emphasis landing on the words that carry the argument. Speed that costs comprehension is negative value however impressive it sounds.

nodes.name: Flowing
nodes.desc: Recording both sides of the round in columns so every argument can be tracked to whoever last answered it. A dropped argument you had a response to reads exactly like a concession, which is why this is a foundation.

nodes.name: Research & Evidence
nodes.desc: Finding sources that say what you need and cutting them without misrepresenting them. The cards that win rounds are qualified, recent, and say the thing in their own words rather than in your paraphrase.

nodes.name: Active Listening
nodes.desc: Hearing what was actually argued rather than the argument you prepared for. Most novice rebuttals answer a case the opponent did not run, which costs the speech and hands the judge a reason to discount you.

nodes.name: Citing Sources
nodes.desc: Author, qualification and date, said out loud, every time. It is mechanical, it is checkable, and an evidence challenge you cannot answer loses more than the card was ever worth.

nodes.name: Case Building
nodes.desc: A constructive that is internally consistent, fits the time, and anticipates the three responses everybody runs. Writing the blocks to those responses while you write the case is what makes the second speech survivable.

nodes.name: Time Allocation
nodes.desc: Deciding before you stand which arguments get ninety seconds and which get ten. Spending four minutes on the contention you enjoy and running out of time on the one that decides the round is the classic loss.

nodes.name: Refutation
nodes.desc: Naming the argument, saying why it fails, and saying what follows — rather than reading a card at it and moving on. The third part is the one that gets skipped and the one a judge writes down.

nodes.name: Cross-Examination
nodes.desc: Asking questions with a destination, and getting the concession on the record so you can use it later. Cross is not scored directly, which is why the answers matter more than looking clever while asking.

nodes.name: Spotting Fallacies
nodes.desc: Recognising the move rather than merely disliking the conclusion — correlation offered as cause, a burden quietly shifted, a term redefined mid-round. Naming it is worth less than showing what it lets the opponent skip.

nodes.name: Weighing Impacts
nodes.desc: Explaining why your impact decides the round even if theirs is also true — on magnitude, probability or timeframe. This is the hinge of the whole tree: below it you win arguments, above it you win rounds.

nodes.name: Framework & Theory
nodes.desc: Arguing about how the round should be judged before arguing inside it. A framework nobody contests decides everything downstream, which is why conceding one early is so much more expensive than it feels.

nodes.name: The Rebuttal Speech
nodes.desc: The last speech, where you stop covering everything and tell the judge the two things that decide it. Going for everything is the most common way to lose a round you were winning on the flow.

nodes.name: Value Debate
nodes.desc: Rounds decided on a criterion rather than on consequences, where the moral framework is the contested ground. It demands actual familiarity with the philosophy, because a judge who knows it will notice a name used as decoration.

nodes.name: Policy Rounds
nodes.desc: Plans, disadvantages, counterplans and solvency, at speed and at volume of evidence. The research burden is unlike any other event, and organisation of the files is a real competitive advantage rather than tidiness.

nodes.name: Reading the Judge
nodes.desc: Adjusting speed, jargon and what you go for based on the paradigm in front of you. Running a technical round in front of a lay judge is a strategy error that no amount of argument quality recovers from.

nodes.name: The Tournament
nodes.desc: Six preliminary rounds in a day, both sides of a resolution you may not agree with, against cases you have never seen. Everything below converges here, and stamina turns out to be a competitive skill in its own right.

nodes.name: Budgeting
nodes.desc: Knowing what comes in, what goes out and what is left before the month decides for you. Almost every money problem that is not an income problem is solved at this node.

nodes.name: Tracking Spending
nodes.desc: Recording where it actually went rather than where you assumed. Two months of honest records changes more behaviour than any amount of resolve.

nodes.name: Saving & Buffers
nodes.desc: Money set aside before it can be spent, starting with enough to absorb a broken boiler. The buffer is what stops a small emergency from becoming an expensive debt.

nodes.name: Debt & Interest
nodes.desc: What borrowing costs, and why compounding runs against you exactly as hard as it runs for you. The rate and the term together decide the total, and the monthly payment hides both.

nodes.name: Credit
nodes.desc: How lenders decide what you can borrow and at what price. Boring habits build it, and the score is a summary of your record rather than a judgement about you.

nodes.name: Taxes
nodes.desc: What is owed, when, and which reliefs exist. Marginal rates are the piece most people have wrong: earning more never leaves you with less overall.

nodes.name: Income & Earning
nodes.desc: Salary, self-employment and everything irregular, seen after tax and after the costs of earning it. Comparing offers on gross pay alone is how people take a pay cut by accident.

nodes.name: Value & Price
nodes.desc: What something costs to make, what it is worth to a buyer, and why those two rarely meet in the middle. Pricing from cost alone leaves money on the table or prices you out entirely.

nodes.name: Bookkeeping
nodes.desc: Every transaction recorded twice, so the books have to balance. Four hundred years old, still the standard, and the reason an error announces itself rather than hiding.

nodes.name: Financial Statements
nodes.desc: Three views of one business: what it owns, what it earned, and what actually moved. Reading them together is the skill, because each one alone can be made to look fine.

nodes.name: Cash Flow
nodes.desc: Money in the account by the date it is needed, which is not the same as being profitable. Profitable businesses fail from running out of cash more often than from anything else.

nodes.name: Business Models
nodes.desc: Who pays, for what, how often, and what it costs to serve them. Most failed ventures had a product and never had an answer to the second half of that sentence.

nodes.name: Customers
nodes.desc: Who has the problem, how badly, and what they do about it today. Talking to twenty of them beats a year of planning, and is the step that gets skipped for being uncomfortable.

nodes.name: Unit Economics
nodes.desc: What one customer earns and what one customer costs to win and serve. If the second is bigger, growth makes things worse, which is a lesson usually learned expensively.

nodes.name: Risk
nodes.desc: What could go wrong, how likely, and what it would cost. Insurance, reserves and diversification are three answers, and knowing which risks you are keeping is the point.

nodes.name: Structures & Contracts
nodes.desc: The legal form of a venture, what it protects, and what a contract is actually promising. Reading the termination and liability clauses first is the habit worth acquiring.

nodes.name: Negotiation
nodes.desc: Finding the deal both sides prefer to no deal. Knowing your walk-away point beforehand is most of it, and asking what the other side needs beats arguing about what you want.

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.desc: Deciding what to do and, harder, what not to. A strategy that does not rule anything out is a list of ambitions with a better name.

nodes.name: Compounding
nodes.desc: Growth on growth, which is unremarkable for five years and startling over forty. Every other idea in this tree is a footnote to how much the time in the market matters.

nodes.name: Inflation
nodes.desc: Money losing purchasing power quietly. Cash under a mattress is not a neutral choice; it is a small guaranteed loss every year, which reframes what "safe" means.

nodes.name: Risk & Return
nodes.desc: Higher expected returns come with a wider range of outcomes, including bad ones. Anything advertising the first without the second is either misunderstood or misrepresented.

nodes.name: Time Horizon
nodes.desc: When the money is actually needed, which decides almost everything else. Money required in two years and money required in thirty are two different problems with different answers.

nodes.name: Emergency Fund
nodes.desc: Several months of expenses somewhere boring and immediately reachable. It exists so that an unexpected bill does not force a sale at the worst possible time.

nodes.name: Asset Classes
nodes.desc: Shares, bonds, property, cash and the rest, each with a different shape of return and risk. Understanding what an asset actually is, and who pays you, comes before any decision about it.

nodes.name: Shares
nodes.desc: Part-ownership of a business, with a claim on what is left after everybody else is paid. That last clause is why they return more on average and fall further when things go wrong.

nodes.name: Bonds
nodes.desc: Lending money for a fixed return, where the risks are default and rates moving. Their price falls when interest rates rise, which surprises people who bought them for safety.

nodes.name: Diversification
nodes.desc: Spreading holdings so no single failure matters much. It is the one thing in investing that reduces risk without reducing expected return, which is why it gets called the only free lunch.

nodes.name: Funds & Index Tracking
nodes.desc: Buying a slice of hundreds of holdings in one purchase. Tracking a whole market cheaply beats most active management over long periods, and the evidence for that is not close.

nodes.name: Fees & Costs
nodes.desc: Percentages that sound trivial and compound exactly like returns do, in the wrong direction. One percent a year over a working life is a substantial fraction of the final total.

nodes.name: Tax-Efficient Saving
nodes.desc: Accounts and wrappers that change what is owed on growth and income. Using the allowance you already have is usually worth more than any change to what is held inside it.

nodes.name: Pensions & Retirement
nodes.desc: Money locked away for decades, often with an employer contribution and tax relief attached. Declining a matched contribution is turning down part of your salary.

nodes.name: Property
nodes.desc: A large, illiquid, borrowed-against, undiversified asset that people also live in. The leverage cuts both ways and the transaction costs make it a poor short-term holding.

nodes.name: Insurance
nodes.desc: Paying a small certain cost to avoid a rare catastrophic one. Insure what would be unrecoverable and self-insure what would merely be annoying.

nodes.name: Behaviour
nodes.desc: Not selling in a crash and not buying at a peak. Investor returns lag fund returns, and the gap is entirely this node rather than any question of selection.

nodes.name: Asset Allocation
nodes.desc: The split between kinds of asset, which drives most of the variation in outcomes. Deciding it in advance is also the mechanism that makes rebalancing possible.

nodes.name: Rebalancing
nodes.desc: Selling what has grown and buying what has not, on a schedule rather than on a feeling. It enforces the discipline of buying low precisely when it feels wrong.

nodes.name: Scams & Red Flags
nodes.desc: Guaranteed returns, urgency, complexity and anything that resists a simple question. The pitch is always about the upside; the tell is what happens when you ask about liquidity.

nodes.name: A Financial Plan
nodes.desc: Goals, timescales, contributions and the rules you will follow when markets move. Written down in advance, because the point of a plan is that it exists before it is needed.

nodes.name: Scarcity & Choice
nodes.desc: Limited means against unlimited wants, which makes every choice a choice against something. The whole subject is the study of that trade-off at different scales.

nodes.name: Opportunity Cost
nodes.desc: The value of the best thing you did not do. It is the concept that changes how decisions are made once it is genuinely internalised, and the one most often quoted without being used.

nodes.name: Incentives
nodes.desc: People respond to what they are rewarded for, including in ways nobody intended. Most policy failures are a rule that was obeyed exactly as written.

nodes.name: Supply & Demand
nodes.desc: Two schedules of willingness meeting at a price. It is a model rather than a law, and its value is in predicting the direction of a change rather than the level of anything.

nodes.name: Elasticity
nodes.desc: How much quantity responds to a change in price. It decides who really pays a tax, which is rarely the person the tax is written against.

nodes.name: Market Structures
nodes.desc: From many small sellers to one, and what changes about price and quantity along the way. Competition is a spectrum, and almost nothing real sits at either end.

nodes.name: Market Failure
nodes.desc: Where prices leave something out: pollution, public goods, information nobody shares. Most economic arguments about policy are arguments about whether one of these is present.

nodes.name: Behavioural Economics
nodes.desc: What people actually do, as opposed to what a perfectly rational agent would. Losses looming larger than equivalent gains is the finding with the widest reach.

nodes.name: Game Theory
nodes.desc: Decisions where the outcome depends on what somebody else decides. The prisoner dilemma is the standard example because individually sensible choices produce a jointly worse result.

nodes.name: Measuring an Economy
nodes.desc: Output, income and expenditure as three routes to one total. What the headline figure excludes — unpaid work, depletion, distribution — is as informative as what it counts.

nodes.name: Growth
nodes.desc: More output per person over time, driven mainly by productivity rather than by effort. Small differences in rate compound into enormous differences in living standards within a lifetime.

nodes.name: Employment
nodes.desc: Who is working, who is looking, and who has stopped looking. The headline rate omits the last group, which is why it can improve while things get worse.

nodes.name: Money & Banking
nodes.desc: What money is, and the fact that most of it is created by commercial banks lending. That mechanism is the part that is genuinely surprising the first time.

nodes.name: Inflation
nodes.desc: A general rise in prices, from demand, from costs, or from expectations feeding themselves. Its costs are unevenly distributed, which is why it is politically explosive at low levels.

nodes.name: Monetary Policy
nodes.desc: A central bank moving interest rates and the quantity of money to steer demand. It acts with a long and variable delay, which is what makes it so hard to get right.

nodes.name: Fiscal Policy
nodes.desc: Government spending and taxation as levers on the economy. Debt matters relative to the size of the economy and the rate on it, not as an absolute number.

nodes.name: International Trade
nodes.desc: Comparative advantage, and why two countries can both gain even when one is better at everything. The aggregate gain is real and so is the fact that it is not shared evenly.

nodes.name: Development
nodes.desc: Why some countries are rich and others are not, and what actually changes it. Institutions, geography and history all compete for the explanation, and the honest answer uses all three.

nodes.name: Inequality
nodes.desc: How income and wealth are distributed and how that changes over generations. Wealth is far more concentrated than income everywhere, and mobility is what makes the difference bearable or not.

nodes.name: Economic Data
nodes.desc: Finding the series, checking how it is constructed, and noticing revisions. Most confident economic claims in public are made about a number nobody has read the definition of.

nodes.name: Thinking Like an Economist
nodes.desc: Asking about incentives, margins and what the alternative was, while remembering the models are simplifications. The discipline is useful precisely to the degree it stays aware of what it left out.

nodes.name: The Problem You Solve
nodes.desc: What somebody was struggling with before this existed. Marketing that starts from features rather than from that struggle is a description rather than a reason to buy.

nodes.name: Audience
nodes.desc: Who specifically, in enough detail to know where they already spend their attention. Everybody is not an audience; it is the phrase that precedes a campaign that reaches nobody.

nodes.name: Customer Research
nodes.desc: Asking people about their behaviour rather than their intentions. What somebody did last month predicts far better than what they say they would do.

nodes.name: Positioning
nodes.desc: The space you occupy in the mind of a buyer, relative to the alternatives, including doing nothing. Being second-best at everything loses to being clearly first for a narrower group.

nodes.name: Messaging
nodes.desc: Saying the thing in words your audience already uses. Clarity beats cleverness reliably, and the test is whether a stranger can repeat what you do after one reading.

nodes.name: Brand
nodes.desc: The set of associations people carry about you, built by consistency over time. A logo is the smallest part of it and the part most often mistaken for the whole.

nodes.name: Copywriting
nodes.desc: Words that get one specific action taken. Lead with the benefit, keep the sentences short, and cut every phrase that would survive being deleted.

nodes.name: Content
nodes.desc: Being useful before asking for anything. It compounds slowly and it is the only channel that keeps working after you stop paying for it.

nodes.name: Search
nodes.desc: Being found by people already looking for the answer. Intent is what makes search traffic valuable, and matching the page to the question is most of the work.

nodes.name: Social Channels
nodes.desc: Platforms where attention is rented rather than owned, and where the rules change without notice. Pick the one your audience is on rather than all of them badly.

nodes.name: Email & Owned Audience
nodes.desc: A list you can reach without an intermediary deciding whether to show it. The most durable asset in marketing, and the one that survives every platform change.

nodes.name: The Funnel
