nodes.desc: The path from never having heard of you to buying, and the drop at each step. Fixing the worst step beats adding traffic to the top, and it is usually far cheaper.

nodes.name: Landing Pages
nodes.desc: One page, one audience, one action. Everything that is not helping somebody take that action is competing with it, including navigation you added out of habit.

nodes.name: Paid Advertising
nodes.desc: Renting attention, measured against what a customer is worth. It scales what already works and reliably accelerates the failure of what does not.

nodes.name: Analytics
nodes.desc: Deciding which numbers actually indicate progress and watching those. Traffic and impressions flatter; activation, retention and revenue per visitor tell you something.

nodes.name: Testing
nodes.desc: Comparing two versions properly, with enough traffic to tell them apart. Most reported wins are noise called early, which is worse than not testing at all.

nodes.name: Retention
nodes.desc: Keeping the customers you already have, which costs a fraction of finding new ones. A leaking bucket makes acquisition an expensive way to stand still.

nodes.name: Pricing & Offers
nodes.desc: What to charge, how to package it and when to discount. Price communicates as much as it collects, and cutting it is the fastest way to change what you are understood to be.

nodes.name: Ethical Persuasion
nodes.desc: The line between making something easy to choose and making it hard to refuse. Manufactured urgency and awkward cancellation work in the short run and are how trust is spent.

nodes.name: Marketing Strategy
nodes.desc: A coherent plan across positioning, channels and budget, with a stated view of who you are not for. The tactics are interchangeable; the choice of which battle to fight is not.

nodes.name: Managing Yourself
nodes.desc: Reliable follow-through on your own commitments before asking anybody to rely on you. A manager who drops things teaches the team that dropping things is acceptable.

nodes.name: Listening
nodes.desc: Hearing what somebody actually said, including the part they were reluctant to say. Most management problems are visible weeks earlier to somebody who was asked and listened to.

nodes.name: Setting Expectations
nodes.desc: Saying what good looks like and by when, before the work starts. A surprising share of underperformance is a person doing exactly what they understood was wanted.

nodes.name: One to Ones
nodes.desc: A regular, protected conversation that belongs to the other person. Cancelling it repeatedly says more about your priorities than anything you would say in it.

nodes.name: Feedback
nodes.desc: Specific, timely and about the work. Saved for a review six months later it is no longer feedback, it is a verdict on something nobody could still fix.

nodes.name: Delegation
nodes.desc: Handing over the outcome and the authority, not the task and the instructions. Keeping the interesting work is the most common way a new manager stalls both the team and themselves.

nodes.name: Prioritising
nodes.desc: Deciding what the team will not do this quarter. A list where everything is important is a list that has not been prioritised, whatever order it is in.

nodes.name: Planning Work
nodes.desc: Breaking an objective into work with owners and dates that somebody actually believes. Estimates are ranges, and treating one as a commitment is how a plan becomes a fiction.

nodes.name: Running Meetings
nodes.desc: A purpose, the right people and a decision at the end. The best improvement most teams can make is deleting half of them and writing the update instead.

nodes.name: Decision Making
nodes.desc: Knowing which decisions are reversible and moving fast on those. Saying who decides, before the discussion, prevents the meeting that ends with everybody assuming somebody else will.

nodes.name: Hiring
nodes.desc: Defining the role, running a fair process and testing for the work itself. A slow hire is expensive and a wrong hire is far more expensive, mostly to the people around them.

nodes.name: Onboarding
nodes.desc: The first month deciding whether somebody becomes effective or quietly disengages. A first task that ships, and one named person to ask anything, does most of the work.

nodes.name: Coaching & Growth
nodes.desc: Helping somebody get better at what they want to be better at, which may not be what you want from them. Asking beats telling, and the payoff is longer than any one quarter.

nodes.name: Conflict
nodes.desc: Two people who both have a point, addressed early and in person. Avoided, it does not fade; it becomes a fact about the team that new joiners inherit.

nodes.name: Performance Problems
nodes.desc: Naming the gap, agreeing what changes, and following through either way. Handled clearly it is a kindness; left alone it is unfair to the person and to everybody covering for them.

nodes.name: Trust & Safety
nodes.desc: A team where bad news travels upward quickly. It is built by how you react the first few times somebody tells you something you did not want to hear.

nodes.name: Process & Systems
nodes.desc: Enough structure that the work does not depend on you remembering. Every process has a cost, and the ones added after a single incident are the ones to review.

nodes.name: Measuring a Team
nodes.desc: Choosing indicators that do not distort behaviour when people know they are being measured. Any single number will be gamed eventually, including by well-intentioned people.

nodes.name: Leading Change
nodes.desc: Moving a group to a new way of working while the current one is still running. Explaining why, repeatedly and to individuals, is most of the job.

nodes.name: Leadership
nodes.desc: Setting direction people choose to follow, and being the same person under pressure as when things are calm. Authority comes with the title; this does not.

nodes.name: Capture
nodes.desc: Writing everything down the moment it appears, in one place you trust. The value is not the list; it is that nothing is being held in working memory where it costs attention all day.

nodes.name: Tasks Worth Writing
nodes.desc: A task that names a physical next action rather than a topic. "Sort out the insurance" sits untouched for weeks; "find the renewal email" gets done in four minutes.

nodes.name: Deciding the Day
nodes.desc: Choosing a small number of things for today, in the morning or the night before. A list of thirty is not a plan; it is a way of guaranteeing the day ends in a sense of failure.

nodes.name: Prioritising
nodes.desc: Separating what is urgent from what actually matters, and doing the second before the first has finished shouting. Most days are spent entirely on urgent items belonging to other people unless this is deliberate.

nodes.name: Estimating Time
nodes.desc: Guessing how long something will take and then checking. Everybody underestimates, consistently, and the only fix is a record of how wrong you were last time.

nodes.name: Time Blocking
nodes.desc: Putting work in the calendar rather than on a list, so it has to compete with everything else for actual hours. A list pretends time is infinite; a calendar refuses to.

nodes.name: Batching
nodes.desc: Grouping similar work so the setup cost is paid once. Email four times a day rather than continuously is the standard example, and the one with the largest effect.

nodes.name: Starting
nodes.desc: Getting past the first two minutes, which is where most procrastination actually lives. Shrinking the first step until it is faintly ridiculous is the reliable trick.

nodes.name: Procrastination
nodes.desc: Usually avoidance of a feeling rather than laziness: the task is ambiguous, or the outcome is frightening. Naming which one it is suggests the fix, and discipline alone rarely does.

nodes.name: Habits
nodes.desc: Behaviour that no longer requires a decision, built with a cue, a small action and a consistent time. Starting far too small is what makes one stick.

nodes.name: Energy & Rhythms
nodes.desc: Matching demanding work to the hours you are actually sharp. Scheduling analytical work into your worst two hours daily is a hidden and enormous tax.

nodes.name: The Weekly Review
nodes.desc: An hour to empty the inbox, look at every commitment and choose the coming week. It is the maintenance that keeps a system trustworthy, and the first thing dropped when things get busy.

nodes.name: Notes & Reference
nodes.desc: Somewhere to put things you will want later but do not have to act on. Keeping reference material out of the task list is what stops the list becoming unreadable.

nodes.name: Goals
nodes.desc: A small number of outcomes with a date and a defined finish. Goals without a next action are wishes, and goals without a review are forgotten by February.

nodes.name: Projects
nodes.desc: Anything that takes more than one action, broken down far enough that the next step is obvious. A stalled project is nearly always one whose next action was never defined.

nodes.name: Saying No
nodes.desc: Declining early and clearly rather than agreeing and delivering late. Every yes is a no to something with less of a voice, usually your own work.

nodes.name: Tools
nodes.desc: The smallest set of tools that supports the habits. Reorganising the system is itself a satisfying form of procrastination, and switching apps has never once been the problem.

nodes.name: Reflection
nodes.desc: Looking back at what worked and what did not, on purpose and in writing. Without it, the same week is repeated with more effort applied to it.

nodes.name: A System You Trust
nodes.desc: Everything captured, reviewed regularly, and reliable enough that nothing is being remembered. That trust is the point of the whole tree: it is what makes it possible to work on one thing without the rest of it nagging.

nodes.name: How Attention Works
nodes.desc: A limited resource that refills with rest and is spent by switching. Understanding that switching has a cost, rather than believing in multitasking, is what makes the rest of this tree worth doing.

nodes.name: Naming Distractions
nodes.desc: Keeping a note of what pulled you away for a week. It is nearly always a shorter and more specific list than expected, which makes it fixable.

nodes.name: Environment
nodes.desc: A place where the default is work: the phone in another room, the browser closed, the door shut. Changing the surroundings beats resisting them every time.

nodes.name: Notifications
nodes.desc: Turning off everything that is not a person needing an answer now, which is almost all of it. Each interruption costs far longer than it takes, because attention has to be rebuilt.

nodes.name: Focus Sessions
nodes.desc: A fixed block with one task and a timer running. The length matters less than the commitment not to switch inside it, and twenty-five minutes is a starting point rather than a rule.

nodes.name: Single-Tasking
nodes.desc: One thing until it is finished or the block ends. It feels slower and finishes more, which is unintuitive enough that most people need to measure it once to believe it.

nodes.name: Starting Rituals
nodes.desc: A short, repeated sequence that signals work is beginning. Same place, same time, same first action removes the negotiation about whether to start.

nodes.name: Deep Work
nodes.desc: Ninety minutes or more on something cognitively demanding, with nothing else touched. Almost all work that is genuinely difficult is produced in blocks like this and almost nobody schedules them.

nodes.name: Shallow Work
nodes.desc: Email, admin and coordination, which are necessary and expand to fill whatever space is left. Giving them a fixed window is what stops them eating the day.

nodes.name: Context Switching
nodes.desc: The cost of picking up a different task, which is paid in minutes of reloading state. It is why five projects in one day gets less done than two, with more effort.

nodes.name: Flow
nodes.desc: The state where the work carries itself, reached when difficulty roughly matches skill. It cannot be forced and it can be arranged for: clear goal, no interruptions, the right level of hard.

nodes.name: Tolerating Boredom
nodes.desc: Not reaching for a phone in a queue. Attention trained to expect stimulation at every gap will not sit still for two hours of hard work when it is asked to.

nodes.name: Digital Minimalism
nodes.desc: Deciding what each tool is for and removing the rest. Applications are designed by large teams to hold attention, and treating that as a fair fight is the mistake.

nodes.name: Breaks
nodes.desc: Real breaks between blocks, away from a screen. A break spent scrolling restores very little, which is why people finish a day of them still feeling drained.

nodes.name: Working with Energy
nodes.desc: Putting the hardest work where your attention is best and admin where it is not. Most people have two or three genuinely sharp hours, and spend them on email.

nodes.name: Handling Interruptions
nodes.desc: Capturing the thing and returning, rather than following it. Telling somebody when you will be free is more effective than being unreachable and less costly than stopping.

nodes.name: Protecting the Calendar
nodes.desc: Defending contiguous hours from being sliced into unusable fragments. Four meetings spread across a day cost far more than four in a row, and only one of those is negotiable.

nodes.name: Rebuilding Attention
nodes.desc: Extending how long you can concentrate, deliberately and gradually, as a trainable capacity. Reading a long book is unfashionable and remains the most effective exercise for it.

nodes.name: Measuring Focus
nodes.desc: Recording hours of real concentration rather than hours at a desk. The number is always lower than expected, and it is the only one that correlates with output.

nodes.name: A Focused Working Life
nodes.desc: Structuring weeks around the work that needs depth rather than fitting it into the gaps. It is a set of arrangements defended repeatedly, not a personality trait somebody has.

nodes.name: Planning Study
nodes.desc: Deciding what to study when, against the date it is needed. Working through material in the order it appears in a book is a plan by default rather than a decision.

nodes.name: Reading to Learn
nodes.desc: Previewing the structure, asking questions, then reading for the answers. Passive reading from the first line produces a feeling of familiarity that is easily mistaken for knowledge.

nodes.name: Note-Taking
nodes.desc: Notes in your own words, shorter than the source. Transcribing what was said keeps the hands busy and the understanding untested.

nodes.name: Retrieval Practice
nodes.desc: Closing the book and trying to produce the answer. Difficult, unpleasant, and by a wide margin the best-supported study technique there is.

nodes.name: Spaced Repetition
nodes.desc: Reviewing just before you would forget, at growing intervals. It converts a fact learned once into a fact you still have in June, for a fraction of the total time.

nodes.name: Interleaving
nodes.desc: Mixing problem types instead of doing thirty of one kind. Performance in the session gets worse and retention afterwards gets better, which is why almost nobody does it voluntarily.

nodes.name: Explaining It
nodes.desc: Teaching the material to somebody, or to an empty room. The point where the explanation stalls is precisely the gap that rereading would have hidden.

nodes.name: Understanding vs Memorising
nodes.desc: Knowing why something follows, so it can be reconstructed rather than recalled. Some things genuinely must be memorised, and knowing which is a decision worth making explicitly.

nodes.name: Practice Problems
nodes.desc: Working problems without the solution visible, then checking. Reading a worked solution and nodding is the most reliable way to be surprised in an exam.

nodes.name: Learning from Mistakes
nodes.desc: A record of what you got wrong and why, revisited. Most people mark, feel bad and move on, which throws away the most information-dense part of the session.

nodes.name: Memory Techniques
nodes.desc: Mnemonics, stories and places for material that is arbitrary. Enormously effective on lists and sequences, and no substitute for understanding anything with a structure.

nodes.name: Summarising & Mapping
nodes.desc: Compressing a topic onto one page and drawing what connects to what. The compression is where the learning happens; the page afterwards is mostly a souvenir.

nodes.name: Deep Study Sessions
nodes.desc: Long uninterrupted blocks on difficult material, which is what hard subjects require. Two focused hours outperform six with a phone on the desk, and it is not close.

nodes.name: Study Groups
nodes.desc: Working with others, which is excellent for explaining and testing and terrible for first exposure. It needs a stated purpose or it becomes a social event with books open.

nodes.name: Finding Material
nodes.desc: Past papers, textbooks, lectures and problem sets, chosen for the question you actually have. Past papers are consistently the most underused resource available.

nodes.name: Revision Timetables
nodes.desc: A schedule across weeks that revisits everything more than once. Building a beautiful timetable is itself a well-known form of procrastination, so keep it to twenty minutes.

nodes.name: Exam Technique
nodes.desc: Reading the question, allocating time by marks, and writing what is being asked for. A large fraction of lost marks are technique rather than knowledge.

nodes.name: Exam Nerves
nodes.desc: Practising under timed conditions so the state is familiar, and having a plan for going blank. Preparation reduces anxiety far more effectively than reassurance does.

nodes.name: Keeping What You Learned
nodes.desc: Occasional review after the exam, which is what separates a subject you studied from one you know. Almost all of it goes within months otherwise, whatever the grade said.

nodes.name: Teaching Yourself
nodes.desc: Learning something with no course, no deadline and nobody checking. It needs every skill in this tree at once, and it is the one that keeps working for the rest of your life.

nodes.name: Reliability
nodes.desc: Doing what you said by when you said, or saying early that you cannot. It is unglamorous and it is the reputation everything else is built on.

nodes.name: Email & Messages
nodes.desc: Writing so the reader knows what is wanted from them in the first two lines. A message that buries the request under context gets answered late or not at all.

nodes.name: Writing at Work
nodes.desc: Documents that survive being skimmed: conclusion first, headings, and a summary somebody could act on alone. Most workplace writing is read by people looking for one thing.

nodes.name: Meetings
nodes.desc: Knowing why you are there, contributing, and leaving with an owner and a date attached to anything decided. A meeting with no decision should have been a message.

nodes.name: Following Up
nodes.desc: A short written record of what was agreed, sent afterwards. It takes five minutes and it is what prevents the most common failure mode of collaborative work.

nodes.name: Working with Others Remotely
nodes.desc: Writing things down, being explicit about status, and not assuming everybody saw the thread. Distributed work fails on unstated assumptions rather than on technology.

nodes.name: Presenting
nodes.desc: One clear message, slides that support rather than duplicate you, and a rehearsal out loud. Reading your own slides aloud is the most common and most avoidable failure.

nodes.name: Asking Good Questions
nodes.desc: Saying what you tried, what you expected and what happened. It respects the time of whoever answers and usually solves the problem while you are writing it.

nodes.name: Receiving Feedback
nodes.desc: Listening, asking for specifics, and separating the work from yourself. Getting defensive is normal and expensive, because it teaches people to stop telling you things.

nodes.name: Making Work Visible
nodes.desc: Keeping a record of what you did and its effect, and sharing progress without being asked. Good work that nobody knows about is indistinguishable from no work at review time.

nodes.name: Working Across Teams
nodes.desc: Understanding what other groups are measured on, which explains most of what looks like obstruction. Finding the shared interest is faster than escalating.

nodes.name: Managing Your Workload
nodes.desc: Being explicit about what will slip when something is added. Silently absorbing everything ends in missed commitments, and by then the choice has been made for you.

nodes.name: Deliberate Skill Growth
nodes.desc: Choosing what to get better at rather than absorbing whatever the job happens to teach. Time at a desk is not experience; repeated practice on hard things is.

nodes.name: Professional Relationships
nodes.desc: Staying in touch with people you worked well with, before you need anything. Most jobs arrive through weak connections rather than through applications.

nodes.name: CV & Portfolio
nodes.desc: What you did, at what scale, with what result. Responsibilities describe a job description; outcomes describe you doing it.

nodes.name: Job Searching
nodes.desc: A targeted small number of applications beats a hundred generic ones. Reading the posting properly and answering it specifically is most of what gets a reply.

nodes.name: Interviewing
nodes.desc: Structured answers with a situation, what you did and what resulted. Prepared stories beat improvisation, and questions you ask them are assessed as closely as your answers.

nodes.name: Negotiating an Offer
nodes.desc: Knowing the range, asking once, politely and specifically. The conversation is uncomfortable for a few minutes and compounds for years, in both directions.

nodes.name: Changing Direction
nodes.desc: Moving to different work by finding the overlap and building the missing piece publicly. Sideways moves inside a place you are known are usually the cheapest route.

nodes.name: Deciding What You Want
nodes.desc: Working out what you actually want from work — the conditions, not the title. It is the question this whole tree is in service of and the one most easily deferred indefinitely.

nodes.name: Observation
nodes.desc: Drawing what is there rather than what you know is there. The symbol your hand wants to produce for an eye is the single largest obstacle, and defeating it is most of learning to draw.

nodes.name: Shape & Proportion
nodes.desc: Getting the big relationships right before any detail. Measuring by comparison — this is twice that — fixes more work than any amount of careful rendering.

nodes.name: Line
nodes.desc: Confident marks that vary in weight and say something. A line drawn quickly from the shoulder reads better than one assembled from hesitant strokes, even when it is less accurate.

nodes.name: Value & Light
nodes.desc: Light and dark, which do far more work than colour does. Squinting collapses a scene into a few values, and a picture that works in those will work in anything.

nodes.name: Form & Volume
nodes.desc: Making a flat mark look like a solid object under a light. Once you can see the planes turning away from the source, shading stops being guesswork.

nodes.name: Perspective
nodes.desc: Depth on a flat surface, built from a horizon and vanishing points. The rules are simple and unforgiving: one wrong eye level makes an entire drawing feel off without anybody being able to say why.

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.desc: Arranging things inside the frame so the eye goes where you want and stays. It is decided in the first thirty seconds with thumbnails, not rescued in the last hour.

nodes.name: Colour
nodes.desc: Hue, saturation and value as three separate dials. Nearly every muddy result is a saturation problem, and nearly every flat one is a value problem wearing colour.

nodes.name: Materials
nodes.desc: What pencil, ink, paint or pixels each do well and badly. Learning one medium properly teaches more than sampling six, because the limits are what force decisions.

nodes.name: Gesture
nodes.desc: Catching the movement and weight of a subject in seconds. Timed studies teach it, and the point is not to produce a good drawing but to stop drawing outlines.

nodes.name: Anatomy
nodes.desc: The structure under the surface: what a shoulder actually does and where a hip sits. Knowledge is what makes a figure convincing when reference is not available.

nodes.name: Depth & Atmosphere
nodes.desc: Contrast, detail and colour dropping off with distance. It is the difference between a scene that has air in it and a set of objects at different sizes.

nodes.name: Stylisation
nodes.desc: Choosing what to exaggerate and what to leave out. Convincing stylisation is a deliberate departure from something understood, which is why it comes after the observational nodes.

nodes.name: Critique
nodes.desc: Assessing your own work against what you intended, and hearing somebody else do it. Turning the piece upside down or looking in a mirror shows what your eye has stopped seeing.

nodes.name: Working from Reference
nodes.desc: Using photographs and life as material rather than as something to copy. Several references combined and understood beats one traced, and it shows immediately.

nodes.name: Sketch to Finish
nodes.desc: Thumbnails, then a value study, then colour, then detail. Working in that order means the expensive mistakes are found while they cost minutes.

nodes.name: A Body of Work
nodes.desc: Enough finished pieces for the consistencies to become visible. Style is noticed in retrospect across a body of work rather than chosen in advance for a single piece.

nodes.name: Mileage
nodes.desc: Drawing regularly and badly for long enough that the hand catches up with the eye. Nothing else in this tree substitutes for it, and everybody who can draw did this part.

nodes.name: Mark Control
nodes.desc: Straight lines, smooth curves and ellipses that close, drawn from the shoulder. Dull warm-up exercises that quietly determine whether everything later looks confident or scratchy.

nodes.name: Construction
nodes.desc: Building a subject from simple solids before refining it. Drawing through the forms, including the parts you cannot see, is what keeps an object coherent from any angle.

nodes.name: Sight Measuring
nodes.desc: Using a pencil at arm length to compare angles and lengths. It feels mechanical and it is how accurate drawings get made without tracing.

nodes.name: Still Life
nodes.desc: Objects that hold still under a light you control. The ideal training ground precisely because nothing moves and every error is yours.

nodes.name: Shading
nodes.desc: Turning form with value: core shadow, reflected light, cast shadow. The edge between light and shadow tells the viewer more about the surface than the darkness does.

nodes.name: Texture & Surface
nodes.desc: Making a thing look like metal, cloth or skin. It is mostly about how sharp the highlights are and how quickly value changes, not about drawing every detail.

nodes.name: Figure Drawing
nodes.desc: The human body from life, starting with gesture and ending with structure. Weight, balance and where the ribcage sits relative to the pelvis carry the whole drawing.

nodes.name: Portraits
nodes.desc: Likeness, which lives in proportion and placement rather than in careful features. Get the skull and the spacing right and the face appears; get them wrong and no eyelash saves it.

nodes.name: Hands & Feet
nodes.desc: The parts everybody hides behind pockets. Simplified into a box for the palm and wedges for the fingers, they become drawable rather than a wall.

nodes.name: Perspective in Practice
nodes.desc: Putting constructed objects into a believable space, including the ones at odd angles. Establish the horizon first; everything else is measured against it.

nodes.name: Environments
nodes.desc: Landscapes and interiors, where the subject is space rather than an object. Depth comes from overlapping shapes and falling contrast far more than from detail.

nodes.name: Ink & Line Work
nodes.desc: Committing without an eraser, and building value from hatching. The discipline of no undo teaches decisiveness faster than any other medium.

nodes.name: Paint Handling
nodes.desc: Mixing, loading a brush and laying down an edge you meant. Most early painting problems are consistency and brush pressure rather than colour choice.

nodes.name: Colour Mixing
nodes.desc: Getting a specific colour from a limited palette, and keeping it clean. A restricted palette produces more harmonious work than a full set, and teaches faster.

nodes.name: Painting from Life
nodes.desc: Working outdoors or in front of the subject with the light changing. The time limit forces simplification, which is the lesson rather than a nuisance.

nodes.name: Digital Painting
nodes.desc: Layers, brushes and undo, which speed everything up and remove the pressure that taught decisiveness. Fundamentals transfer completely; the shortcuts do not replace them.

nodes.name: Composing a Picture
nodes.desc: Deciding what the picture is of and removing everything competing with it. Thumbnail several arrangements before committing hours to the first idea.

nodes.name: Master Studies
nodes.desc: Copying good work to find out how a decision was made. Analytical copying — asking why an edge is soft there — teaches what admiring never will.

nodes.name: Finished Work
nodes.desc: Taking pieces all the way to done, repeatedly, rather than accumulating strong studies. Finishing is a separate skill and the one that turns practice into a body of work.

nodes.name: The Brief
nodes.desc: What this is for, who it is for and what it has to achieve. Design without a brief is decoration, and most disagreements about taste are really about an unwritten one.

nodes.name: Visual Hierarchy
nodes.desc: Deciding what somebody sees first, second and third, and making the page say so. Size, weight and space do the work; if everything is emphasised, nothing is.

nodes.name: Space
nodes.desc: The empty parts, which are doing as much work as the full ones. Grouping by proximity is the cheapest way to make a layout comprehensible before a single line is drawn.

nodes.name: Typography
nodes.desc: Choosing typefaces and setting them so text is comfortable to read. Line length, line height and size do more for readability than the choice of face, and are noticed less.

nodes.name: Grids & Alignment
nodes.desc: An invisible structure everything lines up to. Most amateur layouts are fixed by alignment alone, and most professional ones are built on a grid nobody notices.

nodes.name: Colour in Design
nodes.desc: A small palette used consistently, with contrast that survives a bad screen. Colour as the only carrier of meaning fails for a tenth of readers, which is why it never carries meaning alone.

nodes.name: Contrast & Legibility
nodes.desc: Text that stays readable in sunlight, at distance and for eyes that are not yours. There are measurable thresholds for it, and passing them is a floor rather than an aspiration.

nodes.name: Layout
nodes.desc: Arranging everything into a whole that reads in the right order. The eye follows size, then contrast, then position, and a layout is a plan for that journey.

nodes.name: Imagery & Icons
nodes.desc: Pictures and symbols that carry meaning rather than fill space. An icon without a label is a guess for anybody who has not met it before.

nodes.name: Identity
nodes.desc: A coherent visual voice across everything a thing produces. Consistency does more for recognition than any individual mark, however good the mark is.

nodes.name: Design Systems
nodes.desc: Decisions made once and reused: spacing, type scale, components. It is what keeps a growing product from becoming forty slightly different buttons.

nodes.name: Users & Tasks
nodes.desc: Who is doing what, under what pressure, on what device. Designing for yourself is the default failure mode, and watching one real person use it cures it instantly.

nodes.name: Flows & Structure
nodes.desc: The sequence of screens or steps somebody moves through. Most usability problems are structural, and no amount of visual polish will fix a flow that asks for things in the wrong order.

nodes.name: Wireframing
nodes.desc: Rough structure before any styling, so the conversation is about arrangement rather than colour. Deliberately ugly, because polish invites feedback about the wrong thing.

nodes.name: Prototyping
nodes.desc: Something clickable enough to test an idea before it is built. The cheapest prototype that answers the question is the right one, and it is usually cheaper than people expect.

nodes.name: Accessibility
nodes.desc: Usable by keyboard, by screen reader and by somebody with a tremor or in bright sun. Designed in it costs little; retrofitted it costs a rebuild.

nodes.name: Motion
nodes.desc: Movement that explains what happened rather than decorating it. Fast, purposeful and skippable, because motion that cannot be turned off makes some people ill.

nodes.name: Usability Testing
nodes.desc: Watching five people attempt a task without help. It finds most of the serious problems, and the hardest part is staying silent while somebody struggles.

nodes.name: Critique & Iteration
nodes.desc: Presenting work against the brief and changing it in response. Defending every decision is as unproductive as accepting every note, and the brief is what settles which is which.

nodes.name: Craft
nodes.desc: The last ten percent nobody consciously notices and everybody feels: consistent spacing, considered edge cases, empty states that say something useful. It is what separates competent from finished.

nodes.name: Seeing Light
nodes.desc: Noticing direction, quality and colour before raising a camera. Photography is a subject about light that happens to involve a machine, and this is the node that decides everything else.

nodes.name: The Frame
nodes.desc: Deciding what is in and what is out, and where the edges cut. Moving your feet does more for a photograph than any adjustment made afterwards.

nodes.name: Exposure
nodes.desc: Aperture, shutter and sensitivity as three ways to get the same brightness. They are a triangle because changing one forces another, and each has a side effect that is the actual creative choice.

nodes.name: Aperture & Depth of Field
nodes.desc: How much of the scene is sharp. Wide open isolates a subject and closed down keeps a landscape crisp, and both are decisions rather than settings.

nodes.name: Shutter & Motion
nodes.desc: Freezing action or letting it blur on purpose. The slowest speed you can hand-hold is a rule of thumb worth knowing and worth breaking deliberately.

nodes.name: Sensitivity & Noise
nodes.desc: Trading grain for the ability to shoot in less light. A slightly noisy sharp photograph beats a clean blurred one every time, which is why this dial moves first indoors.

nodes.name: Focus
nodes.desc: Putting the sharpness exactly where it belongs, which for a portrait is the near eye. Autofocus is excellent at deciding wrongly with great confidence.

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.desc: Arranging the frame so the eye goes where you want: lines, balance, and what the background is doing. Most disappointing photographs are compositionally busy rather than technically wrong.

nodes.name: Colour & White Balance
nodes.desc: Telling the camera what white is, because light is rarely neutral. Getting it right in the file makes every later adjustment easier and more convincing.

nodes.name: Raw & Files
nodes.desc: Keeping the sensor data rather than a processed picture. It costs storage and buys latitude in the shadows and the white balance that a compressed file has already thrown away.

nodes.name: Lenses
nodes.desc: Focal length as a decision about perspective, not about zoom. A wide lens close and a long lens far away frame the same subject and describe entirely different spaces.

nodes.name: Natural Light
nodes.desc: Working with what the sky gives: the hour, the weather and which way the window faces. Overcast is soft and forgiving, and midday sun is the hardest light most people insist on using.

nodes.name: Artificial Light
nodes.desc: Adding light and controlling where it falls. One light off the camera, bounced or diffused, is a bigger jump in quality than any body or lens.

nodes.name: Portraits
nodes.desc: Photographing people, which is half technical and half making somebody comfortable. Direction beats instruction: giving them something to do beats telling them to relax.

nodes.name: Street & Documentary
nodes.desc: Photographs of life as it happens, which requires anticipation and nerve. Being unobtrusive matters more than any camera, and knowing the local rules and courtesies matters more than both.

nodes.name: Landscape
nodes.desc: Big scenes where light and timing do the work and patience is the technique. A tripod and returning to the same spot at a different hour are the two habits that improve it most.

nodes.name: Editing
nodes.desc: Adjusting exposure, contrast and colour to finish what the file started. Restraint is the skill; the strongest edits are usually local and small.

nodes.name: Editing Down
nodes.desc: Choosing the two frames worth showing out of three hundred. Ruthlessness here does more for how your work is seen than anything you can do to an individual photograph.

nodes.name: Working in a Series
nodes.desc: Photographs that mean more together than apart. It is the shift from taking good pictures to saying something, and it is what a body of work is made of.

nodes.name: Output & Print
nodes.desc: Getting an image out of a screen and onto paper or a wall at the right size. Colour management and print size change what an image is, and a photograph is not finished until it exists somewhere.

nodes.name: Story
nodes.desc: Somebody wanting something and meeting resistance. Every technical decision below this exists to serve it, and no amount of craft rescues a sequence with nothing at stake.

nodes.name: Scenes
nodes.desc: A unit of story in one place and time, which should end somewhere different from where it started. If nothing changed, the scene is a conversation rather than a scene.

nodes.name: Shots & Framing
nodes.desc: Wide, medium and close, and what each tells the audience about distance and importance. Changing shot size is punctuation, and using it without reason reads as noise.

nodes.name: Coverage
nodes.desc: Shooting a scene from enough angles that it can be cut together. Missing coverage is discovered in the edit, when returning to the location is no longer possible.

nodes.name: Continuity & the Line
nodes.desc: Keeping screen direction and physical detail consistent between takes. Crossing the imaginary line between two characters makes them appear to swap sides, and audiences feel it even when they cannot name it.

nodes.name: Camera Movement
nodes.desc: Pans, tilts, dollies and handheld, each carrying a different feeling. A move should be motivated by something in the scene; movement for its own sake is the most common early habit to lose.

nodes.name: Lenses & Depth
nodes.desc: Focal length changing how close the audience feels and how compressed the space looks. It is a storytelling choice more than a technical one, made before the tripod goes down.

nodes.name: Exposure for Video
nodes.desc: Shutter angle tied to frame rate, so motion looks the way audiences expect. It is the constraint that makes filters necessary outdoors rather than optional.

nodes.name: Lighting
nodes.desc: Shaping a scene with key, fill and separation. Where the shadows fall does more for mood than the colour of anything, and one flag is often worth two more lights.

nodes.name: Production Sound
nodes.desc: Getting a microphone close and the room quiet. Audiences forgive a soft picture and switch off bad audio within seconds, which reverses the order most people buy equipment in.

nodes.name: Directing Actors
nodes.desc: Giving performers an objective rather than a line reading. What the character wants from the other person in the room produces performance; describing an emotion produces imitation.

nodes.name: Planning a Shoot
nodes.desc: Shot lists, storyboards and a schedule that acknowledges how long lighting takes. Planning is what buys the time to be creative when something inevitably goes wrong.

nodes.name: Editing
nodes.desc: Choosing what to show and for exactly how long. The film is genuinely made here, and the most common improvement is cutting in later and out earlier on every shot.

nodes.name: Pacing & Rhythm
nodes.desc: How fast the film feels, which is about information rather than shot length. A scene drags when the audience already knows what it is being told.

nodes.name: Transitions
nodes.desc: How one scene becomes the next, and why almost all of them should be a cut. A transition is a statement about the relationship between two scenes, not a decoration between them.

nodes.name: Colour Grading
nodes.desc: Matching shots to each other first, then giving the whole thing a look. Consistency across a scene matters far more than any stylistic grade laid over it.

nodes.name: Sound Design & Mix
nodes.desc: Atmosphere, effects, music and dialogue balanced against each other. Sound carries emotion more reliably than picture, and silence used deliberately is the most underused tool available.

nodes.name: Documentary
nodes.desc: Finding the story in material you did not script, with the ethical questions that come with representing real people. The edit is where the film is written.

nodes.name: Making a Short
nodes.desc: Taking one thing from idea to finished, at whatever scale you can actually complete. One finished short teaches more than five abandoned features.

nodes.name: A Body of Work
nodes.desc: Enough finished films for the recurring concerns and choices to become visible. Style is what is left after several films, not a decision made before the first one.

nodes.name: Pulse & Tempo
nodes.desc: Feeling a steady beat and holding it without drifting. Everything rhythmic sits on this, and playing with a metronome exposes immediately how steady you actually are.

nodes.name: Rhythm
nodes.desc: Dividing the beat into patterns and placing notes precisely inside it. Counting out loud feels childish and remains the fastest way to fix a rhythm you keep fluffing.

nodes.name: Reading Notes
nodes.desc: Turning a position on the stave into a pitch without counting up from the bottom line. Recognition needs to become instant, because the moment it does, sight reading stops being arithmetic.

nodes.name: Dynamics & Articulation
nodes.desc: How loud, and how each note is started and released. This is most of what separates a performance from a correct sequence of pitches.

nodes.name: Scales
nodes.desc: The ordered set of pitches a piece draws from, and the pattern of steps that defines each type. Practising them is partly theory and partly the most efficient technique exercise there is.

nodes.name: Intervals
nodes.desc: The distance between two pitches, named by size and quality. Attaching each one to a song you already know is the trick that makes them recognisable by ear rather than by counting.

nodes.name: Keys & Signatures
nodes.desc: Which notes a piece has agreed to use, declared once at the start. The circle of fifths turns fifteen separate facts into one picture worth being able to draw from memory.

nodes.name: Chords
nodes.desc: Three or more notes sounding together, built by stacking intervals. Major, minor, diminished and augmented are four different feelings produced by moving one note a semitone.

nodes.name: Inversions
nodes.desc: The same chord with a different note at the bottom. What changes is not the harmony but the smoothness of the movement, which is what voice leading is about.

nodes.name: Progressions
nodes.desc: Chords in sequence, and why a handful of orders keep reappearing across centuries and genres. Tension and release is the whole mechanism, and cadences are where it resolves.

nodes.name: Ear Training
nodes.desc: Naming what you heard: intervals, chord qualities, and eventually whole progressions. Five focused minutes daily beats an hour a week, and it is the skill the other seven are worth less without.

nodes.name: Sight Reading
nodes.desc: Playing something you have never seen, in time, without stopping. Improved only by reading new material constantly and accepting that it will be rough.

nodes.name: Modes
nodes.desc: The same seven notes started from a different degree, giving seven distinct colours. Hearing dorian as its own thing rather than as a displaced major scale is the point.

nodes.name: Harmony
nodes.desc: How independent lines combine, and the conventions that make some combinations sound intentional. Voice leading — moving each part as little as possible — explains most of the rules.

nodes.name: Musical Form
nodes.desc: The architecture of a piece: what repeats, what contrasts, and where it returns. Hearing structure while listening is what makes long pieces feel navigable rather than endless.

nodes.name: Improvisation
nodes.desc: Making music in real time inside a set of constraints. It is far less mysterious than it looks: a vocabulary of phrases, deep familiarity with the changes, and the nerve to commit.

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.desc: Writing music that goes somewhere. Craft rather than inspiration — a good idea developed properly beats four good ideas laid end to end.

nodes.name: Performance
nodes.desc: Playing for other people, under pressure, and communicating something. A separate skill from playing well alone, and one that only performing actually trains.

nodes.name: Holding the Guitar
nodes.desc: Posture, the angle of the neck and where the thumb sits behind it. Nearly every early complaint about hand pain or muted strings is a posture problem wearing a technique costume.

nodes.name: Tuning
nodes.desc: Getting the six strings to their pitches, by ear and by tuner. Learning to hear when two strings are close but wrong is worth more than the tuner, because it trains the ear you will use for everything else.

nodes.name: Strings & Frets
nodes.desc: The names of the open strings and the fact that one fret is one semitone. Everything about the neck follows from those two facts, though it takes months for that to feel true.

nodes.name: Open Chords
nodes.desc: The first handful of shapes, played cleanly with every string sounding. Getting one shape perfect teaches more than getting five approximately, because the standard is what you will unconsciously keep.

nodes.name: Chord Changes
nodes.desc: Moving between shapes in time, which is a completely separate skill from forming them. Practise the change itself rather than the chords either side, and always with a beat running.

nodes.name: Strumming
nodes.desc: The right hand keeping a constant motion and choosing which passes hit the strings. Keeping the arm moving through the gaps is what makes a pattern feel steady rather than stitched together.

nodes.name: Rhythm Guitar
nodes.desc: Playing so somebody else could sing over you without counting. Being the timekeeper is the job, and it is why the least showy player in a band is often the most important one.

nodes.name: Picking
nodes.desc: Hitting single notes deliberately, alternating down and up. Anchoring, angle and how far the pick travels decide speed far more than practice hours do.

nodes.name: Fingerstyle
nodes.desc: Thumb on the bass, fingers on the melody, played at once. It is the point where one guitar starts sounding like two parts rather than one accompaniment.

nodes.name: Barre Chords
nodes.desc: One finger flattening across all six strings so a shape becomes movable. Brutal for a few weeks, and the moment it works you have every key rather than the four you could reach before.

nodes.name: Power Chords & Palm Muting
nodes.desc: Two notes with the third left out, and the heel of the hand damping the strings. Deliberately ambiguous harmony, which is exactly why it sits under distortion better than a full chord.

nodes.name: Scales on the Neck
nodes.desc: Patterns that move without changing shape, because the neck is regular. Learning them as shapes is fast and learning where the root sits inside each shape is what makes them usable.

nodes.name: Pentatonic Positions
nodes.desc: Five boxes that cover the whole neck and connect to each other. Most lead playing in popular music lives here, and joining the boxes is what stops solos sounding trapped in one position.

nodes.name: Bends & Vibrato
nodes.desc: Pushing a string sideways to raise its pitch, and shaking it to give the note life. Bending to the right pitch rather than approximately is what separates expressive from sour.

nodes.name: Slides, Hammers & Pulls
nodes.desc: Sounding notes with the fretting hand alone. The connected legato line it produces is a different voice from picking every note, and phrasing usually wants both in the same bar.

nodes.name: Capo & Transposing
nodes.desc: Moving the nut up the neck so familiar shapes play in a different key. Invaluable for singers, and worth understanding as transposition rather than as a shortcut you do not have to think about.

nodes.name: Tone & Effects
nodes.desc: Pickups, amplifier settings and the small number of pedals that matter. Most of the tone people chase is in the hands, and the rest is gain staging rather than the brand of anything.

nodes.name: Learning by Ear
nodes.desc: Working a song out from the recording instead of from a tab. Slow, frustrating and the single highest-yield practice there is, because it trains the connection tabs let you skip.

nodes.name: Improvising
nodes.desc: Playing lines over changes as they go past. Phrasing and space matter far more than speed, and the players who sound best are usually leaving the most room.

nodes.name: Arranging a Song
nodes.desc: Deciding what one guitar plays of a piece written for a band. Choosing what to leave out is the skill; a good arrangement implies the missing parts rather than cramming them in.

nodes.name: Playing for People
nodes.desc: Playing under pressure, recovering from a mistake without stopping, and holding an audience. Only performing trains it, and the first several times are supposed to be bad.

nodes.name: Sitting & Hand Shape
nodes.desc: Bench height, a relaxed arm and fingers curved as though holding a ball. It looks fussy and it is what decides whether an hour of practice leaves you sore.

nodes.name: The Keyboard
nodes.desc: Twelve keys repeating, with the black-key groups as landmarks. The layout is the clearest picture of music theory anybody has drawn, which is why theory is easier at a piano than anywhere else.

nodes.name: Fingering
nodes.desc: Which finger plays which note, decided in advance and written in. Chosen well it makes a passage possible; chosen ad hoc it guarantees a different mistake every run.

nodes.name: Reading the Treble Staff
nodes.desc: Turning a position on the upper stave straight into a key, without counting up from the bottom line. It has to become recognition rather than arithmetic before anything else works.

nodes.name: Reading the Bass Staff
nodes.desc: The second stave, with different lines meaning different notes. Learning it thoroughly rather than by relating everything to the treble is what stops the left hand lagging for years.

nodes.name: Hands Together
nodes.desc: Two independent parts at once, which is the first genuinely difficult thing the instrument asks. Practising each hand until it is automatic, then joining them slowly, is the only route that reliably works.

nodes.name: Scales & Arpeggios
nodes.desc: The standard patterns, with the thumb passing under smoothly. Boring, and they are where evenness and finger independence actually come from.

nodes.name: Chords & Voicings
nodes.desc: Playing three or more notes together, and choosing which order to stack them in. The same chord voiced differently is the difference between muddy and open, especially low on the keyboard.

nodes.name: The Sustain Pedal
nodes.desc: Lifting the dampers so notes ring on. The technique is changing it just after the new harmony arrives rather than with it, and holding it through a chord change is the single most audible beginner error.

nodes.name: Touch & Dynamics
nodes.desc: Controlling volume and attack with the speed of the key rather than the force of the arm. Being able to play one hand louder than the other is what makes a melody sing over its accompaniment.

nodes.name: Sight Reading
nodes.desc: Playing something unseen, in time, without stopping to correct. Improved only by reading new material constantly and accepting that it will be rough, which is why so few people build it.

nodes.name: Rhythmic Independence
nodes.desc: Hands playing different rhythms at once, up to three against two. Learned as one combined pattern first, then felt as two, because counting both at speed is not something anybody manages.

nodes.name: Phrasing
nodes.desc: Shaping a line so it has direction, a high point and an ending. It is what makes a correct performance musical, and it is decided before the piece is up to speed, not after.

nodes.name: Harmony at the Keyboard
nodes.desc: Seeing the chords inside written music instead of a wall of individual notes. It cuts memorising time dramatically and is what makes playing from a chord chart possible at all.

nodes.name: Memorising
nodes.desc: Holding a piece by structure, harmony and muscle memory at once. Memory that is only in the fingers fails in public, which is why the other two have to be deliberate.

nodes.name: Period & Style
nodes.desc: Baroque, classical and romantic music asking for different touch, pedalling and freedom with the beat. Playing everything the same way is the most common thing that makes an accurate performance sound wrong.

nodes.name: Improvising
nodes.desc: Making something up over a set of changes, which the keyboard layout makes unusually visual. Start with two hands doing very little each; the temptation to fill everything is what kills it.

nodes.name: Accompanying
nodes.desc: Playing under a singer or another instrument: following, supporting and staying out of the way. Knowing when to drop out entirely is most of what makes an accompanist wanted back.

nodes.name: Building Repertoire
nodes.desc: A set of pieces you can actually play today, maintained rather than collected. Three polished pieces beat twenty half-learned ones every time somebody asks you to play something.

nodes.name: Performing
nodes.desc: Playing for people, recovering from a slip without stopping, and communicating something beyond the notes. A separate skill from playing well alone, and one only performing trains.

nodes.name: Breath Support
nodes.desc: Low, quiet breathing and a steady controlled release. It is the engine of the whole instrument, and the fix for more vocal problems than any technique that sounds more interesting.

nodes.name: Posture & Alignment
nodes.desc: A tall spine, a loose jaw and a neck that is not doing any lifting. The throat is a tube, and anything that kinks it changes the sound before any technique gets a chance to.

nodes.name: Warming Up
nodes.desc: Gentle sirens and lip trills that get blood into the folds before demanding anything. Ten minutes beforehand costs less than the two days off that skipping it eventually buys.

nodes.name: Pitch Matching
nodes.desc: Hearing a note and producing that note. Almost nobody is truly tone deaf; most people who believe they are have never been taught to hear the gap and adjust.

nodes.name: Finding Your Range
nodes.desc: The notes available comfortably today, which is not the same as the notes you can reach once. Choosing songs inside it is the fastest improvement most singers ever make.

nodes.name: Tone & Resonance
nodes.desc: Where the sound vibrates once it has left the folds, and how much of it comes out. Volume comes from resonance rather than effort, which is exactly backwards from how it feels.

nodes.name: Vowels & Diction
nodes.desc: Shaping vowels consistently and getting consonants out of the way of them. Sung text lives on the vowels, and words become unintelligible when consonants are late rather than when they are quiet.

nodes.name: Registers
nodes.desc: Chest, head and the mixed sound between them. The break is where the folds change how they vibrate, and smoothing it is a matter of practice at the crossing rather than avoiding it.

nodes.name: Sustain & Control
nodes.desc: Holding a note steady at any volume, and ending it deliberately. A note that sags in pitch as it fades is a breath running out, not an ear failing.

nodes.name: Dynamics
nodes.desc: Singing genuinely quietly without going breathy, and loudly without pushing. The quiet end is the harder one and the one that makes the loud end mean anything.

nodes.name: Rhythm & Timing
nodes.desc: Landing exactly where the beat is, including when the phrase starts before it. Singers drift more than instrumentalists because breath takes time and nobody plans for it.

nodes.name: Ear Training for Singers
nodes.desc: Hearing an interval and singing it cold, without an instrument. This is what lets you hold a part when everything around you is doing something else.

nodes.name: Harmony Singing
nodes.desc: Holding a line a third or a fifth away from the tune while hearing both. The hard part is not finding the note, it is not being pulled onto the melody by the person beside you.

nodes.name: Agility & Runs
nodes.desc: Moving quickly and cleanly between notes so each one is actually there. Built slowly with a metronome, exactly like an instrumental passage, and audibly faked when it is not.

nodes.name: Belting Safely
nodes.desc: Carrying a strong sound high without shouting. It relies entirely on support and a mixed register, and doing it wrong is the fastest way to injure a voice.

nodes.name: Vocal Health
nodes.desc: Hydration, sleep, silence after heavy use, and knowing what hoarseness means. The instrument is tissue and it does not care about the schedule you have committed to.

nodes.name: Style & Interpretation
nodes.desc: Deciding what the song is about and letting that choose the phrasing, weight and where you sit against the beat. Two technically identical performances differ entirely here.

nodes.name: Microphone Technique
nodes.desc: Distance and angle as a volume control, and pulling back on the loud notes. A microphone rewards restraint, and singing at it as though it were a room throws away everything it offered.

nodes.name: Performing
nodes.desc: Singing to people with adrenaline running, which shortens breath and sharpens pitch. Preparation is the answer: rehearse in the state you will be in, not only in the state you like.

nodes.name: Recording Vocals
nodes.desc: Performing to a microphone in a silent room, in pieces, with no audience to lift it. Comping several takes into one is normal practice, and the skill is keeping the result sounding like one performance.

nodes.name: The DAW
nodes.desc: The software everything happens in: tracks, a timeline, transport and a mixer. Learning the shortcuts of one program properly beats trying three, because fluency is what keeps an idea alive.

nodes.name: How Audio Works
nodes.desc: Sample rate, bit depth, and what a waveform on screen actually represents. Knowing why digital audio clips hard rather than gracefully explains most of the rules that follow.

nodes.name: MIDI
nodes.desc: Notes as instructions rather than sound: pitch, timing, length and how hard. It is infinitely editable, which is why an idea gets written in MIDI and committed to audio later.

nodes.name: Tempo & Grid
nodes.desc: Setting a tempo and placing everything against the bar. Quantising fixes timing and flattens feel at the same time, so how much to apply is a musical decision rather than a technical one.

nodes.name: Programming Drums
nodes.desc: Kick, snare and hats laid out to carry a groove. Velocity and small timing shifts are what stop a pattern sounding like a machine, and they matter more than the choice of samples.

nodes.name: Bass & Low End
nodes.desc: The part that ties rhythm to harmony, and the region where a mix most easily turns to mud. Getting kick and bass to share the space is the first real mixing decision anybody faces.

nodes.name: Chords & Melody
nodes.desc: Writing the harmonic bed and the line that sits on top of it. A strong four-chord loop with one good melody beats a clever progression nobody can hum.

nodes.name: Sound Selection
nodes.desc: Choosing sounds that leave room for each other. Half of what people try to fix with equalisation is a choice of two sounds that occupy exactly the same territory.

nodes.name: Synthesis
nodes.desc: Building a sound from oscillators, a filter and an envelope. Learning subtractive synthesis once makes every preset readable and every plugin less mysterious.

nodes.name: Sampling
nodes.desc: Taking recorded audio and playing it as an instrument — chopped, stretched, reversed. The technical part is easy; clearing what you sample from a record is the part that ends projects.

nodes.name: Recording
nodes.desc: Getting a real performance in cleanly: gain staging, microphone placement and a room that is not fighting you. Everything gained here is free, and everything lost here is permanent.

nodes.name: Editing
nodes.desc: Comping takes, trimming, crossfading and tightening timing. Invisible when done well, and the difference between a demo and something that holds attention for three minutes.

nodes.name: Arrangement
nodes.desc: Deciding what happens when, and what drops out so the next section can arrive. Most tracks that feel flat are arrangement problems that no amount of mixing will touch.

nodes.name: Equalisation
nodes.desc: Turning frequency ranges up and down so parts stop competing. Cutting what is not needed goes further than boosting what you want, and both are done in the context of the whole mix.

nodes.name: Compression
nodes.desc: Automatic volume control: threshold, ratio, attack and release. The attack setting is what decides whether a snare keeps its crack, and it is the control most people ignore.

nodes.name: Reverb & Delay
nodes.desc: Putting sounds in a room and at a distance. Predelay and how much low end the effect keeps decide whether a mix sounds spacious or washed out.

nodes.name: Mixing
nodes.desc: Balance, panning and depth so every part is audible and the important one is in front. Start with faders alone; if it does not work there, no plugin is going to rescue it.

nodes.name: Automation
nodes.desc: Changes written into the timeline rather than set once. A static mix is a compromise across three minutes, and moving one fader through a chorus often solves what an hour of processing could not.

nodes.name: Mastering
nodes.desc: The final pass for level, tone and consistency across a release, ideally by fresh ears. It is a polish on a finished mix, not a rescue, and loudness past a point costs dynamics outright.

nodes.name: Finishing & Releasing
nodes.desc: Exporting properly, naming files, keeping stems, and actually putting it out. Deciding a track is done is a skill, and the alternative is a hard drive of things that were nearly finished.

nodes.name: Posture & Setup
nodes.desc: How you sit or stand, where the instrument is, and what is carrying the weight. It decides what is physically possible before technique gets a say, and it is the usual cause of an injury that ends a season.

nodes.name: Warm-Up Routine
nodes.desc: The same ten minutes every time, so that the body arrives at the piece already working. On a competition day it doubles as a familiar thing to do in an unfamiliar building, which is most of its value.

nodes.name: Deliberate Practice
nodes.desc: Isolating the bar that fails, slowing it until it never fails, and only then speeding it up. Playing a piece through from the top is performing, not practising, and an hour of it improves almost nothing.

nodes.name: Tone Production
nodes.desc: The sound itself, before any of the notes are interesting. It is the first thing a panel hears and the thing they can judge in four seconds, which is roughly how long they take to form an impression.

nodes.name: Working with a Metronome
nodes.desc: Finding out where you actually rush, which is never where you think. The hard passage is usually played too slowly and the easy bar after it too fast, and only an external pulse will tell you so.

nodes.name: Sight-Reading
nodes.desc: Playing something in front of you for the first time without stopping. Examined directly in most auditions, and improved only by reading new material daily rather than by getting better at your pieces.

nodes.name: Ear Training
nodes.desc: Hearing an interval, a chord or a wrong note and knowing what it was. It is what lets you correct pitch mid-phrase instead of finding out afterwards from a recording.

nodes.name: Memorisation
nodes.desc: Four memories, not one — muscular, aural, visual and structural — because adrenaline takes the muscular one first. A performer who can only start from the top has one memory and no way back in.

nodes.name: Phrasing
nodes.desc: Deciding where a line is going and shaping it so a listener can hear the destination. Correct notes with no phrasing is the most common thing a jury describes as technically fine and unmemorable.

nodes.name: Ensemble Playing
nodes.desc: Listening across while playing, and following a breath rather than a count. Playing with an accompanist for the first time in the audition itself is the avoidable disaster this node exists to prevent.

nodes.name: Building Repertoire
nodes.desc: A set of pieces at performance standard, kept there, covering the periods a syllabus asks for. Learning a programme from scratch for each competition is why players plateau — nothing ever gets past merely secure.

nodes.name: Recording Yourself
nodes.desc: Hearing what an audience hears, which is impossible while playing. It is uncomfortable, it takes ten minutes, and it is the single highest-yield thing on this tree — every branch above depends on it.

nodes.name: Dynamics & Contrast
nodes.desc: Real range rather than three shades of medium, and the discipline of saving the loudest for where it means something. A recording is usually what reveals that your forte and piano are a great deal closer than intended.

nodes.name: Performance Nerves
nodes.desc: Rehearsing the conditions, not just the piece — playing it cold, first thing, to one person, without a warm-up. Adrenaline cannot be removed, so the training is making the performance survivable while it is present.

nodes.name: Taking Criticism
nodes.desc: Separating what a teacher or panel actually said from how it felt to hear it, and turning it into a practice plan by the next day. Feedback that is agreed with and not acted on is the same as feedback nobody gave.

nodes.name: The Recital
nodes.desc: A programme, in order, without stopping, in front of people who came to listen. Recovering from a slip inaudibly is worth more here than any single difficult passage, because the audience only notices the stopping.

nodes.name: Interpretation
nodes.desc: Having a defensible reason for every choice — tempo, rubato, voicing — grounded in the period and the score rather than in habit. At this level a panel is choosing between players who all have the notes.

nodes.name: Auditions
nodes.desc: Two minutes, possibly behind a screen, possibly stopped partway through. Choosing an excerpt that shows what you do well, and opening in a way that survives the first four seconds, is a strategy problem rather than a musical one.

nodes.name: The Competition Stage
nodes.desc: Rounds, an unfamiliar instrument, a jury with a rubric, and one attempt. Everything below converges here because the stage tests preparation, memory, nerve and interpretation at the same time and gives no second run.

nodes.name: Consistency
nodes.desc: Training on the days you do not want to, at a volume you can repeat next week. It is the only variable that reliably separates people who get results from people who read about them.

nodes.name: Warming Up
nodes.desc: Raising temperature and rehearsing the movement before loading it. Ten minutes that make the session better rather than a ritual performed to avoid guilt.

nodes.name: Movement Quality
nodes.desc: Doing the movement well before doing it heavy or fast. Filming a set is the cheapest coaching available, and almost always shows something different from what it felt like.

nodes.name: Mobility
nodes.desc: Being able to get into the positions the training asks for. Usually a strength problem at the end of a range rather than a tightness problem, which changes what fixes it.

nodes.name: Effort & Intensity
nodes.desc: Knowing how hard a set or an interval actually was, in repeats left or in how hard it was to breathe. Most people train the middle too hard and the top not hard enough.

nodes.name: Progressive Overload
nodes.desc: Asking slightly more of the body over time — more weight, more reps, more distance, better form. Without it, training maintains, which is a legitimate goal but a different one.

nodes.name: Programming
nodes.desc: Deciding in advance what each session is for across a week and a block. A plan written down is what stops every session becoming whatever you felt like on the day.

nodes.name: Rest & Recovery
nodes.desc: The adaptation happens between sessions, not during them. Training more while recovering less is the most common way that progress stops and injuries start.

nodes.name: Sleep
nodes.desc: The single largest recovery variable and the one most often traded away. Nothing in supplementation comes close to the effect of an extra hour, consistently.

nodes.name: Eating for Training
nodes.desc: Enough energy and enough protein to support what you are asking for. Under-eating while training hard produces fatigue that looks like a programming problem.

nodes.name: Hydration
nodes.desc: Enough fluid, and electrolytes when sessions are long or hot. Small deficits reduce performance measurably before thirst becomes noticeable.

nodes.name: Injury & Pain
nodes.desc: Telling soreness from something that needs attention, and modifying rather than stopping entirely. Training around an injury keeps the habit that would otherwise be lost with it.

nodes.name: Tracking Progress
nodes.desc: A log of what was actually done, which is the only reliable memory of it. Trends over months are the signal; any single session is noise.

nodes.name: Goals & Phases
nodes.desc: Choosing what this block is for, because strength, endurance and body composition pull in different directions. Chasing all three at once is how people spend a year unchanged.

nodes.name: Habits & Environment
nodes.desc: Making the session easy to start: kit ready, a fixed time, somewhere close. Motivation is unreliable and arranging your surroundings is not.

nodes.name: Training for Life
nodes.desc: Strength, cardiovascular fitness and balance as the things that decide how the last decades go. The training that matters at sixty is decided at thirty.

nodes.name: Bodyweight Basics
nodes.desc: Push-ups, squats, rows and holds, which build the control that loading later depends on. They are also the fallback that keeps training possible with no equipment at all.

nodes.name: Bracing & Breathing
nodes.desc: Creating pressure through the trunk so the spine stays stacked under load. It is the technique that makes heavy lifting safe, and it is taught last far too often.

nodes.name: The Hinge
nodes.desc: Pushing the hips back with a neutral spine — the pattern under deadlifts, swings and picking anything up. Confusing it with a squat is the most common and most costly error.

nodes.name: Squat
nodes.desc: Sitting between your feet under load, to a depth your hips and ankles allow today. Depth follows mobility rather than willpower, and forcing it is how backs round.

nodes.name: Deadlift
nodes.desc: Lifting a loaded bar from the floor, which trains almost everything at once. It is also the lift where fatigue degrades form fastest, so the last rep decides whether the set was a good idea.

nodes.name: Pressing
nodes.desc: Pushing weight away, overhead and horizontally. Shoulder position at the start decides how much load the joint tolerates, far more than the weight on the bar does.

nodes.name: Pulling
nodes.desc: Rows and chin-ups, which most programmes under-do relative to pressing. Balancing the two is what keeps shoulders healthy over years rather than months.

nodes.name: Carries & Core
nodes.desc: Holding something heavy and walking, plus the anti-rotation work that goes with it. The most direct transfer to real tasks of anything in the gym.

nodes.name: Bars, Dumbbells & Machines
nodes.desc: What each implement is good for. Machines are not cheating; they remove the balance requirement, which is sometimes exactly what a session needs.

nodes.name: Sets, Reps & Load
nodes.desc: How the three interact: heavy and few for strength, moderate and more for size. Total hard sets per muscle per week is the number that predicts progress best.

nodes.name: Rest Between Sets
nodes.desc: Long enough to repeat the effort, which for heavy compound work is minutes rather than seconds. Cutting rest turns a strength session into a conditioning one by accident.

nodes.name: Tempo & Control
nodes.desc: Owning the lowering phase rather than dropping into it. Slower eccentrics build more with less load, which is useful whenever joints are complaining.

nodes.name: Programming
nodes.desc: Sessions arranged so the hard work is spread and recovered from. Beginners progress every session, everybody else progresses across weeks, and confusing the two stalls people for years.

nodes.name: Deloads & Fatigue
nodes.desc: Planned easy weeks that let accumulated fatigue clear. Taken before they are needed they cost nothing; taken after, they are called an injury.

nodes.name: Breaking Plateaus
nodes.desc: Diagnosing whether the block is technique, recovery, nutrition or programming. Adding more work is the usual guess and the least often correct one.

nodes.name: Training for Size
nodes.desc: Volume near failure with enough food to build on. Muscle grows on a timescale of months, and expecting to see it weekly is what makes people abandon working programmes.

nodes.name: Power & Speed
nodes.desc: Moving moderate loads fast, which is a different quality from maximum strength. Trained fresh and stopped the moment bar speed drops, because slow practice trains slow.

nodes.name: Strength Through Range
nodes.desc: Being strong in the positions at the end of a range rather than only in the middle. It is what makes mobility work stick instead of resetting within days.

nodes.name: Peaking & Testing
nodes.desc: Arranging several weeks so that one day is your strongest. Testing maximums often is not training; it is a repeated interruption of it.

nodes.name: Lifting for Decades
nodes.desc: Adjusting the training as the body and the calendar change, so it lasts. Almost nobody regrets going slightly lighter and almost everybody regrets one session they knew they should have stopped.

nodes.name: Aerobic Base
nodes.desc: Easy sustained work, at a pace you could hold a conversation through. It feels too slow to be doing anything and it is the foundation every faster session is built on.

nodes.name: Technique
nodes.desc: Cadence, posture and where the foot lands, or the equivalent in the pool and on the bike. Efficiency means going the same speed for less energy, which is worth more than fitness gains at first.

nodes.name: Breathing
nodes.desc: Rhythmic, relaxed and matched to effort. It is also the most reliable everyday gauge of how hard a session actually is, long before any device tells you.

nodes.name: Effort Zones
nodes.desc: Dividing effort into bands by heart rate, pace or feel. The value is not precision; it is keeping easy days genuinely easy so hard days can be hard.

nodes.name: The Long Session
nodes.desc: One session a week that goes further than the others, built up gradually. It teaches the body to use fat for fuel and teaches you what happens after ninety minutes.

nodes.name: Weekly Volume
nodes.desc: Total time or distance across a week, increased in small steps. Most overuse injuries are a volume jump rather than a technique fault, and they arrive two weeks after the jump.

nodes.name: Intervals
nodes.desc: Hard efforts with recovery between them, which raise the ceiling that base work raised the floor of. One or two sessions a week is the dose; three is how people get injured.

nodes.name: Threshold Work
nodes.desc: Comfortably hard efforts at the pace you could hold for about an hour. It is the single most trainable determinant of endurance performance.

nodes.name: Hills & Resistance
nodes.desc: Strength work disguised as a session, with less impact than flat speed work. Uphill builds power and downhill is where the damage and the skill both live.

nodes.name: Strength for Endurance
nodes.desc: Two sessions a week of heavy, low-rep lifting, which improves economy and resistance to injury. It does not make endurance athletes bulky, which is the fear that keeps most of them from doing it.

nodes.name: Fuelling
nodes.desc: Carbohydrate before and during anything long, practised in training rather than tried on the day. The gut is trainable, and race day is the worst possible place to discover it is not.

nodes.name: Heat, Cold & Altitude
nodes.desc: How conditions change achievable pace and required fluid. Adjusting expectations for the weather is a skill; refusing to is how a good session becomes a bad week.

nodes.name: Training Plans
nodes.desc: Weeks arranged around one goal, with easy weeks built in. Roughly eighty percent easy and twenty percent hard is the distribution that keeps reappearing across sports and levels.

nodes.name: Recovery Between Sessions
nodes.desc: Sleep, food and easy days, which are training rather than the absence of it. Adaptation happens in the gaps, and removing them removes the point of the work.

nodes.name: Common Injuries
nodes.desc: Shins, knees, tendons and the pattern that precedes each. Almost all of them announce themselves quietly for a week before the session that gets blamed.

nodes.name: Pacing
nodes.desc: Distributing effort so the last quarter is the fastest you can make it. Going out too hard is universal, feels correct at the time, and costs more than any tactical error later.

nodes.name: Tapering
nodes.desc: Reducing volume while keeping some intensity in the last couple of weeks. Fitness is already banked; the taper only lets accumulated fatigue clear so it can be shown.

nodes.name: Racing
nodes.desc: Executing a plan while adrenaline argues for a different one. Nutrition, pacing and the willingness to hold back for the first third are decided beforehand or not at all.

nodes.name: Cross-Training
nodes.desc: Swimming, cycling or rowing to keep the engine while a joint recovers. It is what turns an injury from a lost season into a lost month.

nodes.name: Seasons & Longevity
nodes.desc: Building years rather than blocks, with off-seasons that are genuinely off. The athletes who improve for a decade are the ones who allowed themselves to be unfit for a few weeks each year.

nodes.name: Energy Balance
nodes.desc: Energy in against energy out, which decides weight over time regardless of the diet it is wrapped in. Every approach that works does so by changing one side of it, usually appetite.

nodes.name: Macronutrients
